title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
Where we are
By now you’ve:

used an agent to draft a DuckDB pipeline (S6)
written tests for it (S7, S8)
watched OpenCode+free-model and Claude Code+paid-model do the same task side by side (S5)

Today’s question: what does any of this actually cost, and how do you decide, in advance, whether a given model/approach is worth it for a given task?






Question


If your S6 pipeline took 30 seconds and a few cents of API calls on a toy dataset, what happens when the real dataset is 100x bigger? Is the answer “100x the cost”, or something else?

title: Cost & Model Economics
section: Why this matters for you as a researcher
text:
Why this matters for you as a researcher

Agent-driven work has a marginal cost per run, unlike a script you write once and run for free forever.
Grant budgets, RA time, and compute credits are finite — “just ask the agent again” is not free.
As Data Editor of a journal, I see replication packages that quietly assume unlimited API budget. That assumption doesn’t survive contact with a reviewer re-running your pipeline on their own key.
The skill here isn’t memorizing prices (they change monthly) — it’s building the habit of estimating before running.

title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
Tokens, not characters or words

Providers bill per token, not per word or character.
A token is roughly 3/4 of an English word on average, but code, non-English text, and unusual formatting tokenize less efficiently.
Almost all providers separate:

input tokens (prompt: your instructions + context + tool outputs fed back in)
output tokens (what the model generates)

Output tokens are typically priced higher than input tokens (often 3-5x) — generation is more expensive than reading.







Try it


Paste a paragraph of your own writing into a tokenizer (e.g. the OpenAI tokenizer playground, or run opencode with a verbose/debug flag if it reports token counts) and compare token count to word count.

title: Cost & Model Economics
section: Why agent loops cost more than “one prompt”
text:
Why agent loops cost more than “one prompt”
A single chat message is cheap. An agent doing a multi-step task is not one call — it’s many:

system prompt + your instructions (input)
tool definitions available to the agent (input, every single call)
tool call output — e.g. file contents, command output, error messages (input, fed back in)
the model’s reasoning/response (output)
repeat for every tool call in the loop







The key fact


Context accumulates. By the 10th tool call in a session, you are re-paying for the entire conversation history so far as input tokens on every single subsequent call, unless the harness does something (compaction, caching) to reduce it.



This is why a “quick fix” that takes an agent 20 tool calls to find can cost far more than the size of the final diff suggests.

title: Cost & Model Economics
section: Free tier vs paying: a question
text:
Free tier vs paying: a question






Question


Why might the free tier be exactly the right choice for a course exercise, but the wrong choice for a paper you’re submitting to a journal with a two-week reviewer deadline?

title: Cost & Model Economics
section: When is “cheap enough” actually good enough?
text:
When is “cheap enough” actually good enough?
Ask three questions before reaching for the expensive model:

Is the task well-specified? (“rename this column”, “write a regex for X”) — cheap models are fine.
Is the task ambiguous or high-stakes? (interpreting a messy codebook, writing the core estimation routine) — pay for the better model, the time you save debugging usually exceeds the price difference.
Can you verify the output cheaply? If you have a fast, reliable test (S7/S8!), you can afford to let a cheap model guess and check — verification cost is what makes cheap models viable at all. Without tests, you’re trusting a cheap model’s output on faith, which is a bad trade.







This connects back to S7/S8


A good test suite doesn’t just catch bugs — it changes the economics of which model tier you can afford to use.

title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
API models: pros and cons
Pros

No hardware to buy or maintain
Always the current best model, no fine-tuning needed
Pay only for what you use

Cons

Marginal cost scales with usage — no ceiling unless you set one
Your data (prompts, tool outputs, sometimes whole files) leaves your machine
Provider outages, rate limits, deprecations are outside your control
Costs are close to impossible to predict exactly in advance for agentic (multi-step) workflows

title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
Local models: pros and cons
Pros

Zero marginal cost per call once you have the hardware
Data never leaves your machine — relevant for sensitive survey data, embargoed data, IRB constraints
No rate limits, no outages, fully reproducible (pin the exact model weights)

Cons

Upfront hardware cost (GPU with enough VRAM) or cloud rental cost
Local open-weight models currently lag frontier proprietary models on hard reasoning tasks
You maintain the stack (drivers, quantization, serving software)
Your own electricity and setup time are real costs, just not itemized on an invoice

title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
Local vs API: a question






Question


For a research pipeline you’ll run once on a 500-row dataset, is local worth the setup cost? What changes if you’ll run it 10,000 times on similarly-sized batches?

title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
The break-even intuition
Local hardware has a fixed upfront cost; API calls have a cost that scales with volume. There’s a break-even usage volume above which local is cheaper.
\[
\text{break-even calls} = \frac{\text{hardware cost}}{\text{API cost per call}}
\]
This is deliberately naive (ignoring electricity, your time, and quality differences) but it’s the right first-order question to ask before deciding.






Try it


Pick a rough GPU rental price (e.g. $0.50-$2/hour on a cloud provider) and a rough API cost per call for your S6-style task. At what call volume does renting a GPU for the day beat paying per call?

title: Cost & Model Economics
section: The four numbers you need per run
text:
The four numbers you need per run
For any agent-driven step in a pipeline, you can estimate:

Input tokens per call — roughly: prompt + system prompt + accumulated context + any file/data content fed in
Output tokens per call — roughly: length of the expected response (code, summary, analysis)
Number of calls — how many agent turns/tool calls does the task realistically take? (Look at a real transcript from S6/S7/S8 — don’t guess blind.)
Price per token — for input and output separately, for the model tier you plan to use

\[
\text{cost per run} \approx \sum_{\text{calls}} \big(\text{input tokens} \times \text{price}_{\text{in}} + \text{output tokens} \times \text{price}_{\text{out}}\big)
\]

title: Cost & Model Economics
section: Scaling assumptions matter more than the price
text:
Scaling assumptions matter more than the price
The naive instinct is “10x the data, 10x the cost.” That’s often wrong in both directions:

Sub-linear: if the agent writes one query/script that then runs over the full dataset without further agent involvement, the agent cost barely changes — only the compute cost of running the resulting code changes (and that’s not an LLM cost at all).
Super-linear: if bigger data means more edge cases, more debugging turns, more back-and-forth with the agent to fix things that only show up at scale, cost can grow faster than data size.







The habit


Before scaling up, ask: “does the agent do more work at 10x scale, or does my existing code just process more rows?” Those have wildly different cost profiles.

title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
Time is a cost too
Token cost is one axis. Wall-clock time is another, and they don’t always move together:

A cheap model may be slow (long queue times on free tiers) — fine for homework, bad the night before a deadline.
A frontier model may be fast but rate-limited on your account tier.
Local models remove queueing but add your own compute time.

When budgeting a pipeline for a real deadline, estimate time separately from money — a run that’s cheap but takes 6 hours may not be the right choice for a task due in 2.

text:
What you’ll produce (1/2)

title: Cost & Model Economics
text:
What you’ll produce (2/2)

Dollar and time figures: give an actual $ estimate (using a real, current price for the model tier you’d use) and a rough wall-clock time estimate, for both the 10x and 100x scenarios.
One paragraph: would you use the same model for all three scales, or would your choice change? Why?







Where to find real prices


Check the current pricing page for whichever provider you used in S6/S7/S8 (OpenRouter, Google AI Studio, Anthropic, etc.) — prices change often, always use the number as of the day you write the estimate, and cite the date.

text:
Submission






Submission


A short written note (half a page to a page is plenty) alongside your S6/S7/S8 repo — this is not a slide deck, it’s a budgeting memo you could actually hand to a PI or grant officer.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
text:
Where we left off






Recap from Session 4



An LLM is a next-token predictor, trained on huge amounts of text, then fine-tuned with human feedback.
It has no memory between calls, no access to your files, no ability to run code — on its own.
Hallucination is structural: the model always produces some plausible next token, correct or not.





So how does typing a prompt into OpenCode turn into a diff on your screen, touching real files on your disk?
That gap is what today is about: the harness — everything wrapped around the model to make it useful.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
text:
Objectives






By the end of this session you can explain



What a context window is, and why it is finite and expensive.
Conceptually, what “attention” does — no math required.
What a system prompt is and what it’s doing behind the scenes.
What “tool calling” means and why it’s the mechanism that lets a model act.
The full loop: prompt → context assembly → model call → tool call → result → repeat → diff.
Why the same task can cost very differently depending on model + harness choice.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
text:
The layered model, again


From Session 1:

Model — the LLM itself (GPT, Claude, Llama, …)
Harness — the program that talks to the model (OpenCode, Claude Code, Cursor, …)
Tool — a capability the harness exposes to the model (read file, run shell command, edit file, search web)
Skill — a packaged, reusable procedure built on top of tools








Today’s focus


The harness layer. The model is a black box that takes text in and produces text out. Everything else — memory, files, actions in the world — is the harness’s job.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
section: What actually gets sent to the model
text:
What actually gets sent to the model

An LLM API call is just: a block of text in, a block of text out.
Every time you send a message in OpenCode, the harness doesn’t just send your message. It assembles a whole package:

A system prompt: instructions about how to behave, what tools exist, how to format tool calls.
The conversation history so far (your previous messages, the model’s previous replies).
Any tool results from earlier in the session (file contents, command output).
Your new message.



All of that, concatenated into one text blob, is the actual input to the model. The model has no separate “memory” — the entire past of the conversation is re-sent, every single turn.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
text:
The context window






Definition


The context window is the maximum amount of text (measured in tokens, not characters or words) the model can process in a single call — both what goes in and what comes out.





A token is roughly 3/4 of a word (recall Session 4: a chunk of a word, not a whole word).
Typical modern context windows: 128k–1M+ tokens (this changes fast, and providers advertise it as a selling point).
If the assembled input (system prompt + history + tool results + your message) exceeds the window, something has to give: the harness truncates, summarizes, or drops old turns.









Why this matters practically


A long agent session — lots of files read, lots of back-and-forth — can silently fill the context window. The agent starts “forgetting” things you told it 20 turns ago, not because it’s being careless, but because that text is no longer in the window.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
text:
Attention, conceptually
You don’t need the math. You need the idea.







The idea


For every token the model is about to generate, it doesn’t treat every earlier token in the context equally. It computes, on the fly, “how relevant is each earlier piece of text to what I’m producing right now?” — and weighs accordingly.






This is why putting the important instruction at the end of a long prompt often works better than burying it in the middle — the mechanism doesn’t guarantee uniform “reading.”
It is also why irrelevant context isn’t free: every token in the window is a candidate for attention, and more candidates means more room for the model to attend to the wrong thing.
Nothing here is guaranteed or hand-tunable by you — you interact with it indirectly, by controlling what’s in the context and where.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
section: System prompts: the harness’s instructions to the model
text:
System prompts: the harness’s instructions to the model






Definition


A system prompt is a block of text the harness prepends to every conversation, invisible to you by default, that tells the model: who it is, what it can do, and — critically — the exact syntax for calling tools.




A real agent system prompt typically says things like:

“You are a coding assistant operating inside a project directory.”
“You have access to the following tools: read_file, write_file, run_command, edit. To use one, output .”
“Always explain your plan before making changes.” / “Prefer minimal diffs.” / project-specific rules (recall S3’s agent-rules file).



This is why project-level config files (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, OpenCode’s config) matter: they get folded into the system prompt on every single call in that project, shaping every response without you retyping anything.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
section: Tool calling: how a model “does” something
text:
Tool calling: how a model “does” something
The model itself cannot read a file, run git commit, or edit code. It can only produce text.







The trick


The harness tells the model, in the system prompt: “if you want to read a file, output text in this exact format.” The model, being a good next-token predictor trained on this pattern, does exactly that when it decides a file read would help. The harness watches for that pattern, intercepts it, actually runs the file read, and feeds the result back in as a new turn.





So a “tool call” from the model’s point of view is just: producing a specific string of text that looks like a function call. The intelligence is in the harness recognizing and executing it — the model is never touching your filesystem directly.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
text:
The full loop






From prompt to diff — the actual sequence



You type a prompt in OpenCode.
Harness assembles context: system prompt + history + your message.
Harness sends this to the model API.
Model returns text — either a normal reply, or a tool-call pattern (e.g. “read file x.R”).
If it’s a tool call: harness executes it for real (reads the file), appends the result to the context, and goes back to step 3 — without you doing anything.
This repeats — read, edit, run tests, read output, edit again — until the model produces a final reply with no more tool calls.
Harness renders any file edits as a diff on your screen.





What looks like one prompt → one answer is often many model calls chained by the harness, each one re-sending the whole growing context.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
section: Activity: write the loop from memory
text:
Activity: write the loop from memory






5 minutes, pairs


Close this deck. On paper or in a text file, write the prompt-to-diff loop in your own words, in 5 steps or fewer. Then turn to your neighbor and explain it to them out loud — no notes.




Trade papers. Check each other’s version against the slide before this one:

Did they mention the system prompt getting re-sent every turn?
Did they capture that a tool call is text the harness intercepts, not the model directly acting?
Did they show at least one loop-back (tool result feeding into another model call)?



Keep this page — you’ll want it again in Session 11 when we catalogue where agents went wrong across the course.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
section: Why this explains agent behavior you’ve seen
text:
Why this explains agent behavior you’ve seen

Why agents sometimes “forget” earlier instructions → context window pressure, or the instruction got attended to weakly.
Why agents can get expensive fast → every tool-call round-trip re-sends the entire context so far, and cost scales with tokens in and out.
Why a good system prompt / config file makes a noticeable difference → it’s re-injected on every call, unlike something you said once ten turns ago.
Why two harnesses on the same model can behave differently → different system prompts, different tool sets, different strategies for compacting old context when it fills up.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
section: Live demo: same task, two harnesses
text:
Live demo: same task, two harnesses






The task


Starting fixture: scripts/s5-winsorize/winsorize.R. It contains a small, untested function winsorize(x, p = 0.05) that is supposed to cap the bottom p fraction of a numeric vector at the p-quantile and the top p fraction at the 1 - p-quantile, but currently has a bug (the upper cutoff is computed as quantile(x, p) instead of quantile(x, 1 - p), so it caps far too many high values instead of just the top p fraction). Run the identical prompt in both harnesses, in a fresh copy of the same starting directory:

“Look at winsorize.R. Write a testthat test file for winsorize() that checks it correctly caps values at the p and 1-p quantiles, including edge cases. Run the test, and if it fails, find and fix the bug in winsorize(). Show me the diff.”





Run 1: OpenCode + free-tier model (what you use day to day in this course).
Run 2: Claude Code + a paid frontier model (one-off comparison — not what we teach).








Fill this in live, one column per harness





Observation
OpenCode (free)
Claude Code (paid)




Read winsorize.R before writing the test?




Number of tool-call rounds to finish




Did the test fail on first run, as expected?




Found and fixed the actual bug (not a different one)?




Diff quality (minimal / noisy)
















The point of this demo


The model and the harness are separate axes of choice. A better/pricier model does not automatically mean a better harness experience, and vice versa — you are always choosing both. Cost numbers get precise in Session 9; today, just notice that one of these runs was free and the other wasn’t.

title: How Agents Work: Context, Tools, Harnesses
text:
Wrap-up






You should now be able to explain



What happens, mechanically, between typing a prompt and seeing a diff.
Why context windows are finite and why that has practical consequences.
What a system prompt is doing and why project config files matter.
What a “tool call” actually is (text pattern recognized by the harness, not the model reaching into your computer).
Why model choice and harness choice are two separate cost/quality decisions.

title: S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
text:
TipObjectives




Learn the four core building blocks of any language — variable, loop, conditional, function — in both R and Python.
Practice the habit this whole course is built on: have an agent write a first draft, then verify it, try to break it, and write a test that would have caught the bug if it were there.
By the end you should be asking, reflexively, of any code an agent hands you: “where is this wrong, and how do I check?”
© Florian Oswald, 2026

title: S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
section: Why we do this with an agent, not by hand
text:
Why we do this with an agent, not by hand
You could learn these four constructs the old way: read a syntax reference, type it in yourself, get red squiggly lines until it compiles. That’s not how you’ll actually write code anymore. You’ll ask an agent — OpenCode, in this course — to draft something, and your job shifts from “get the syntax right” to “decide whether the result is correct.”
Today we practice exactly that shift, on the simplest possible material, so the habit is cheap to build before the material gets harder in later sessions.
The core loop for the rest of this session, and honestly the rest of the course:

Ask the agent to write something.
Read what it produced. Does it look right?
Try to break it — pick an input the agent probably didn’t think about.
Write a small check (an assert / stopifnot) that would catch the bug if it’s there.
Run it. If it fails, you found something real. Fix it, and keep the check.

title: S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
text:
Setup
Two terminals, one running R, one running python (a REPL, a script, or opencode sessions in each). We use numpy for arrays and pandas for dataframes in the reference section below.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

title: S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
text:
Variables
A variable is a label attached to a value — a number, a string, or any more complex object.

PythonR



x = 12.3
x + 5

17.3





x <- 12.3  # `=` also works at top level, but `<-` is idiomatic
x + 5

[1] 17.3





Where a variable is visible (its scope) matters. A function looks for names it doesn’t recognize locally in the environment where it was defined (this is called lexical scoping), not necessarily where it’s called from:

PythonR



def myfun(y):
    return x + y  # `x` is not a parameter — where does it come from?

myfun(8)

20.3





myfun <- function(y){
    x + y
}
myfun(8)

[1] 20.3





Both work because x was defined earlier in the same scope the function was created in. If you’d never defined x, both would error — try it (comment out the x <- ... / x = ... lines above and re-run).

title: S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
text:
Loops
Loops repeat an operation over a sequence, so you don’t write near-identical statements by hand and don’t have to touch the code again when the input size changes.

PythonR



for i in range(2, 5):
    print(f"this is number {i}")

this is number 2
this is number 3
this is number 4





for (i in 2:4) {
  print(paste("this is number", i))
}

[1] "this is number 2"
[1] "this is number 3"
[1] "this is number 4"





Look closely at what actually printed. If you intended to cover the numbers 2, 3, 4, 5, did you get all four — and are the two bugs even the same bug? They’re not, and that’s the point:

Python’s range(2, 5) is half-open by design: it stops before its second argument, so it yields 2, 3, 4 and silently drops 5. This isn’t a typo, it’s how range always works — the bug is forgetting that convention when translating “2 through 5” into code.
R’s 2:4 is not truncated by : at all — R’s : operator is inclusive on both ends, so 2:5 would correctly give 2, 3, 4, 5. The bug here is a plain wrong literal: whoever (or whatever agent) wrote 2:4 mistyped the upper bound, full stop.

Same visible symptom — one element missing — but two different root causes, in two different places (a language convention vs. a transcription slip). An agent draft can produce either kind, and “it printed one fewer number than expected” doesn’t tell you which one you’re looking at until you read the code.






ImportantExercise 1 — find the bug in each language, then check for it




Before reading further, predict what the two loops above print. Then run them.
Fix both so they print 2, 3, 4, and 5 — but explain in one sentence, per language, why the original was wrong (half-open range convention vs. wrong literal). If your explanation is the same for both, look again.
Write a check — stopifnot() in R, assert in Python — that captures the intended output (e.g. “the loop should touch exactly 4 numbers: 2,3,4,5”) and would fail on the original, unfixed version. Save it; you’ll use the same pattern below.

title: S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
text:
Functions
A function packages a computation so you can reuse it and give it a name that documents intent.

PythonR



def mean_positive(values):
    """Average of the positive numbers in `values`."""
    positives = [v for v in values if v > 0]
    return sum(positives) / len(positives)

mean_positive([1, -2, 3, 4])

2.6666666666666665





mean_positive <- function(values) {
  positives <- values[values > 0]
  sum(positives) / length(positives)
}
mean_positive(c(1, -2, 3, 4))

[1] 2.666667





Run it on [1, -2, 3, 4] and it works fine: 2.6.... Now think about what breaks it before you try it.

title: S2 — Programming Constructs, Agent-Native
section: The exercise: agent draft, then verify, then break it
text:
The exercise: agent draft, then verify, then break it
This is the actual point of today. Below are two small tasks. For each, the “agent draft” columns show code exactly as a first draft from an agent might look — plausible, running, subtly wrong. Don’t just read them: open OpenCode, ask it to write the same function fresh in both languages, and compare what you get against these. Free-tier models sometimes get these exactly right, sometimes reproduce the same bug — either way, work through the seeded version below so everyone in the room breaks the same code at least once.

Task A — mean_positive: average of the positive numbers in a list
This is the function from above. It has a real bug: what happens when there are no positive numbers?

Python (agent draft)R (agent draft)



def mean_positive(values):
    positives = [v for v in values if v > 0]
    return sum(positives) / len(positives)

mean_positive([-1, -2, -3])

ZeroDivisionError: division by zero





mean_positive <- function(values) {
  positives <- values[values > 0]
  sum(positives) / length(positives)
}
mean_positive(c(-1, -2, -3))

[1] NaN





Python raises ZeroDivisionError. R silently returns NaN and moves on — no error at all, which is worse, because a silent NaN can propagate for pages of downstream code before anyone notices.






ImportantExercise 2 — write the test, then fix the function




Write a check that documents the bug before fixing anything:

Python: assert len(positives) > 0, "no positive values in input" (placed before the division).
R: stopifnot(length(positives) > 0).

Confirm the check fails (raises) on [-1, -2, -3] / c(-1, -2, -3) in the original function.
Decide what the correct behavior should be — raise clearly? Return NA/None on purpose? There’s no single right answer, but the agent’s draft picked one silently, without telling you. Fix the function to do what you decided, on purpose, and keep the check as a permanent guard.





Task B — running_total: cumulative sum of a list

Python (agent draft)R (agent draft)



def running_total(values):
    total = 0
    result = []
    for v in values[1:]:  # look closely at the slice
        total += v
        result.append(total)
    return result

running_total([10, 20, 30])

[20, 50]





running_total <- function(values) {
  total <- 0
  result <- c()
  for (v in values[-1]) {  # look closely at the indexing
    total <- total + v
    result <- c(result, total)
  }
  result
}
running_total(c(10, 20, 30))

[1] 20 50





Both versions drop the first element (values[1:] in Python skips index 0; values[-1] in R excludes the first element) — so a 3-element input silently returns only 2 cumulative totals, and the first one is missing entirely from the running sum. This is the same shape of bug as Task A: it runs without error, produces output that looks like a plausible cumulative sum, and only close reading (or a test on length/first-element) catches it.






ImportantExercise 3 — same pattern, different bug




Predict, then check: what does running_total([10, 20, 30]) return? What should it return? (Hint: length 3, first element 10.)
Write the test first — assert len(running_total([10, 20, 30])) == 3 / stopifnot(length(running_total(c(10,20,30))) == 3) — confirm it fails against the draft.
Fix the function so the test passes. Also add an edge case: what should running_total([]) return? Does your fix handle it? Write a check for that too.

title: S12 — Capstone: An End-to-End Agentic Research Project
section: What “using everything from S1–S11” means, concretely
text:
What “using everything from S1–S11” means, concretely
This is not a checklist to satisfy for its own sake — it’s the minimum standard for a repo you’d hand to a stranger (or an agent, or a JPE replication reviewer) and expect it to just work.







From session
What your capstone repo must show




S1
A git repository, initialized properly, with a sensible .gitignore (no data dumps, no credentials, no OS junk files).


S2
Code that does something nontrivial in at least one of R or Python — variables, loops, conditionals, functions, used because they’re the right tool, not because the rubric demands them.


S3
Standard project layout, no hardcoded absolute paths, a project-level agent config file (e.g. AGENTS.md/opencode.json or equivalent), and a README a stranger could follow cold: what the project answers, how to reproduce it, what depends on what.


S4
Nothing to demonstrate directly — but if your project uses an LLM as a component (e.g. classifying text, extracting structured data), you should be able to say why you don’t fully trust its raw output and what you did about that.


S5
A visible record of how you worked with your agent: prompts that mattered, at minimum one place where you had to intervene because the agent had gone off track.


S6
A real data wrangling step — SQL, dplyr, or Ibis over DuckDB (or an equivalent tool if your data genuinely doesn’t fit that model — ask before assuming).


S7
A unit test suite covering your pipeline’s core transformations.


S8
At least one verification pattern beyond a plain unit test: an invariant check, a golden-output comparison, or an assertion embedded in the pipeline itself.


S9
A short cost note: what it cost (tokens, dollars, time) to run this project, and what it would cost at 10x the data.


S11
An entry in your reproducibility checklist for at least one moment where the agent produced a plausible-but-wrong result in this project, and what caught it.



If your project doesn’t naturally touch one of these (e.g. no spatial component, so S10 is silent) that’s fine — S10 is not in the required list above for exactly that reason. But S1, S3, S6–S9, and S11 should all leave a visible trace in your final repo. If one is missing, say so explicitly in your README rather than hoping nobody notices — an honest “we didn’t get to X, here’s why” is worth more than a silently absent test suite.

title: S12 — Capstone: An End-to-End Agentic Research Project
text:
Timeline
This session runs across the scheduled capstone block(s) plus your own time outside class. A reasonable split:

Propose (before the in-person block). One paragraph: the research question, the data source, why it’s answerable in the time you have. Bring it to class — we’ll sanity-check scope together. A capstone that’s too ambitious to finish honestly is a worse outcome than a small one that’s actually reproducible.
Build (in-person + independent work). Set up the repo (S1/S3 bar) before writing analysis code. Use your agent the way you’ve practiced all course: draft, verify, catch what it gets wrong, write it down.
Verify. Run your own S7/S8-style test suite against your own pipeline. If you can, ask a classmate to try to break it — a bug someone else finds before the presentation is much cheaper than one found live.
Present. A short presentation (roughly 5–8 minutes, format confirmed in class) covering: the question, the pipeline, one thing the agent got wrong and how you caught it, and the cost note.
Peer review. Each project gets reviewed by at least one classmate using the checklist below. This is not a grade — it’s a second pair of eyes doing exactly what S11 practiced: trying to find where a plausible-looking result might actually be wrong.

title: S12 — Capstone: An End-to-End Agentic Research Project
text:
The reproducibility bar (S3 / S11 standard)
This is deliberately close to the standard used for replication packages submitted to an academic journal — the point of S11 was to make that standard feel normal, not exotic, by the time you get here.
A repo that clears the bar:

Clones and runs on a machine that isn’t yours, with no manual path-editing.
Has a README stating: the question, how to reproduce the full pipeline from raw data to final output, and any external dependencies (API keys, packages, data downloads) with instructions for obtaining them.
Has a project-level agent config file, consistent with what you set up in S3.
Separates raw data (or documents how to obtain it, if it can’t be committed) from generated output.
Has a passing test suite that runs as part of, or immediately after, reproducing the pipeline.
Documents, in one place, every point where an agent produced something wrong and what caught it — your S11 checklist, applied to this specific project rather than kept as a general habit.
States the cost of reproducing the full pipeline (S9 note).

title: S12 — Capstone: An End-to-End Agentic Research Project
text:
Peer review guidelines
When reviewing a classmate’s repo, you are standing in for the JPE Data Editor lens introduced in S11: not “is this interesting,” but “can I actually verify this works, and did they tell me the truth about where it might not.”
For each project you review, answer:

Did it actually reproduce for you, following only the README?
Did the test suite pass? Did you try to break anything it didn’t cover?
Is there at least one honestly-reported case of the agent being wrong? Does the fix look right to you, or does it look like the bug is still there?
Is the cost note plausible given what the pipeline does?

Bring written notes (a few sentences per question is enough) to share with the presenter after their talk.

title: S12 — Capstone: An End-to-End Agentic Research Project
text:
A note on scope
The capstone question is yours to choose — this course does not prescribe a dataset or a domain. The bar is on process (does the repo meet the reproducibility standard, does the pipeline have tests, is the agent’s role in the work visible and verified), not on the sophistication of the underlying research question. A simple, fully verified project clears the bar; an ambitious, unverified one does not.

R and Packages

We have been using R packages all the time.
Each time we say library(xyz) we are using external code provided in the xyz package.
You can write your own packages.








What’s the point of Packages?



Extend R functionality.
for researchers: key tool to ensure reproducibilty of findings
for researchers: key tool to organize code in team work





Let’s go through some material from the r-pkgs book!

Building a Toy Package


RStudio for the win

Ok, but…Adding Code??

Let’s add a function to the file R/sayhello.R:

# Notice I'm using = instead of < - because 
# the font of those slides prints it weirdly
hello = function(who){
    paste("hello,",who)
}

Now, if this were a simple R script, we could source the R/sayhello.R file into global space and try this out.
We don’t want to do that here though. 🤨
Instead, we want to load the package, which contains our function.
do load_all():

load_all()

title: Building R Packages
text:
Trying out Code






load_all()



The load_all() function simulates the process of building, installing, and attaching the toypackage package.
This means that all the functions you included in the package will become visible in the global scope (in your console)
This is not in general the case: Later on we will fine-tune which functions are visible to the user, and which ones are not!





Call the function with your name!

hello("Peter")
[1] "hello, Peter"

Great!

title: Building R Packages
text:
Checking the Package

R has a rigid set of rules for what a package needs to look like.
What files should be where, their names and permissions, such that the structure is nicely uniform across all R packages.
Particularly relevant for official packages on CRAN
Do this here often:

check()

This outputs a bunch of things:

It actually builds our package in a separate process - immune from our current workspace
It runs a battery of checks and returns a report:


0 errors ✔ | 1 warning ✖ | 1 note ✖

Editing DESCRIPTION

Open the DESCRIPTION file (or type Ctrl + . and start typing desc)
Fill in the obviously missing contents.

Adding a LICENSE

Use a license, any license (Jeff Atwood)

Let’s
use_mit_license()

title: Building R Packages
text:
Documenting with Roxygen

Go back to the hello function, place the cursor inside the function body, and do Code > Insert Roxygen Skeleton.
You’ll see something like this:

#' Title
#'
#' @param who 
#'
#' @return
#' @export
#'
#' @examples
hello <- function(who){
  paste("hello,",who)
}

Each line starting with #' is part of the docstring.
The roxygen package can separate those blocks from our code, and produce valid R documentation for us! 🤯

title: Building R Packages
text:
Building Documentation

Let’s modify the docstring accordingly.
execute the document() function.
After that, the documentation is visible to us:

?hello
ℹ Rendering development documentation for "hello"

Look in the Help pane in RStudio!

title: Building R Packages
text:
NAMESPACE

Did you notice the @export tag in the docstring?
when we ran document(), roxygen changed the NAMESPACE file based upon that tag.
Go and look at that file!
The contents of NAMESPACE specify what is visible to a user who does library(toypackage).
Try removing the @export tag, and document() again. Look back at NAMESPACE!

check() again!
check()
0 errors ✔ | 0 warnings ✔ | 0 notes ✔

title: Building R Packages
text:
Time to INSTALL the package

Ok, great. Now we have a minimal package that works to a certain extent 🙂.
We must install it into our package library, in order to be able to use it like any other package (same as when we did install.packages("ggplot2"))
Notice that R installs your packages here:


.libPaths()

[1] "/Users/floswald/Library/R/arm64/4.5/library"

👏

title: Building R Packages

New Session - Try it Out!

Restart Rstudio
type into the console

library(toypackage)

and then let’s see our cool 😎 function:

hello("John Spencer Blues Explosion")
[1] "hello, John Spencer Blues Explosion"

title: Building R Packages
text:
Automatically Testing Our Code

We verified ourselves that this works.
We had our own, informal, way to convince ourselves that it works.
We knew which steps we had to follow until we would conclude that “yes, this works”.










The Time Factor


If you come back to this in 2 months time you probably

won’t remember all the steps you have taken (above)
won’t be able to reproduce what you tested today!











The Scale Factor


As your package grows, you will find it hard to come back to all components repeatedly, making sure they all still work as intended (now that they may depend on other parts of your code)

title: Building R Packages
text:
Enter Unit Testing

Automatic Unit Testing or Continuous Integration (CI) is our best response to this.
We still have to design and write the tests, but we can offload the work to run the tasks repeatedly, and automatically, to a helpful infrastructure.

library(devtools)
use_testthat()

then

use_test("sayhello")
• Modify 'tests/testthat/test-sayhello.R'

title: Building R Packages
text:
Writing Unit Tests

Ideally, each function in our R/ folder is covered by a corresponding test.







What Is a Test?


The purpose of a test is to verify that some part of your code, a function in most cases, works as intended.




Modify 'tests/testthat/test-sayhello.R' like so

test_that("hello function works", {
  who = "James T. Kirk"
  expect_equal(hello(who), paste("hello,",who))
})

Ready for 🚀 takeoff?

Running all unit tests

You can run each test file separately to try it out (you must do library(testthat) first)
It’s better practice to test the entire package though:

Using other packages

Most likely our package would depend some other package as well.
Like we could choose the export some of our functions, we now may want to import some functions from elsewhere.

Adding a Vignette

Vignette’s are a great feature of R packages. They are full text introductions of the package to a first time user.
A tutorial for your package.
This is going to be much more verbose and spiked with example input and ouput than the standard documentation.
Often it features the main use case of your package.

Summary






Key Points



RStudio greatly facilitates R package development.
R packages contain code, data and documentation in highly structured fashion.
We are encouraged to run automated unit tests.
It is relatively straightforward to publish the package to github for collaboration.
It is equally straightforward to build and publish a full website with package documentation and vignettes, hosted for free on github.com.

title: S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
text:
Why this session exists
Since S2: “where is this wrong, and how do I check?”

So far: read the code, run it, look at the output — doesn’t scale
Scales even less once an agent writes most of the code and you review it
A unit test writes down “here is what I checked” so it’s checked again automatically, every time the code changes — including every agent edit


This session runs remotely (over video call rather than in person) but is still hands-on: work through it at your own computer, running everything as you go. S8 builds directly on this with property-based tests and golden-output checks; S7 is the foundation.







Objectives



Know what a unit test is, and what it is not worth testing.
Write tests in testthat (R) and pytest (Python) using arrange-act-assert.
Understand fixtures: fixed, known inputs with a known correct output.
Have a first test suite covering real data-wrangling transformations.

title: S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
section: What to test (and what not to bother testing)
text:
What to test (and what not to bother testing)
Rough triage, for code you write and code an agent drafts:
Worth testing:

Your own transformation logic — filtering rules, aggregation formulas, edge cases (empty input, all-invalid input, a single row)
Anywhere a silent decision gets made (a tolerance, a default, a “drop rows where X” rule an agent added without telling you)
Anything embarrassing or costly to get wrong quietly — a mean over the wrong denominator, a join that silently drops rows

Not worth testing:

Well-tested library behavior you’re calling correctly (test your usage, not dplyr::filter()’s internals)
Trivial getters/setters, one-line wrappers with no logic
Anything that varies run-to-run for reasons outside your control (current time, live network) — unless designed around (mocking) — S8 territory


The line isn’t always obvious, and that’s fine — the question to ask is: “if this were subtly wrong, would anything catch it before a reader of my output does?” If the answer is no, write a test.

title: S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
text:
Fixtures
A fixture: a small, fixed, known input, factored out so multiple tests can reuse it and the input is obvious at a glance.
Both languages below build the same four-row table: two polls from pollster A (one valid, one that doesn’t sum to 1), one valid poll from pollster B, one poll from pollster C with an invalid (negative) sample size.

title: S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
text:
Fixtures — R
make_polls <- function() {
  data.frame(
    pollster   = c("A", "A", "B", "C"),
    samplesize = c(1000, 1000, 500, -1),
    remain     = c(0.52, 0.48, 0.50, 0.50),
    leave      = c(0.48, 0.50, 0.50, 0.50),
    undecided  = c(0.00, 0.00, 0.00, 0.00),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

testthat has no special fixture decorator for this kind of case — a plain helper function called at the top of each test_that() block is idiomatic. (For fixtures that need setup/teardown, e.g. a temp file, see withr::local_tempfile() — out of scope today, but worth knowing the name.)

title: S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
text:
Arrange — Act — Assert
Every test below (and every test you should write) has the same three-part shape:

Arrange: build the input — the fixture above.
Act: call the function under test, exactly once, with that input.
Assert: check the output against a value you computed by hand — never a value you got by running the code and copy-pasting whatever it printed.


That third step verifies the code agrees with itself, not that it’s correct — a test whose expected value came from running the code is not a test.

title: S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
text:
Arrange — Act — Assert, in code

R (testthat)Python (pytest)


test_that("check_shares flags rows that sum to 1 as valid", {
  # Arrange
  polls <- make_polls()

  # Act
  out <- check_shares(polls)

  # Assert
  expect_equal(out$share_total, c(1.00, 0.98, 1.00, 1.00))
  expect_equal(out$valid, c(TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, TRUE))
})


def test_check_shares_flags_rows_that_sum_to_one(polls):
    # Arrange: `polls` fixture
    # Act
    out = check_shares(polls)
    # Assert
    # Note: floats need pytest.approx, not `==` -- exact equality on a
    # computed sum passes only "by luck" of binary representation.
    assert out["share_total"].tolist() == pytest.approx([1.00, 0.98, 1.00, 1.00])
    assert list(out["valid"]) == [True, False, True, True]




Notice the 1.00, 0.98, 1.00, 1.00 values in both — those were computed by hand from the fixture above, not generated by running check_shares() and copying its output. Also notice the asymmetry between the two languages: testthat::expect_equal() compares numerics with a small default tolerance built in, so raw values compare safely; pytest’s == does not, so floating-point assertions in Python need pytest.approx() explicitly — forgetting it is an easy way to write a test that’s flaky for the wrong reasons.

title: S7 — Testing & Verification, Part 1: Unit Tests
text:
The full test suites

R: scripts/s7/test-pipeline.R (6 test_that() blocks, 8 expectations)
Python: scripts/s7/test_pipeline.py (6 tests)

Both cover:

Shares summing to 1 → valid; not summing to 1 → invalid
A wider tolerance can let a borderline row through
Invalid rows and non-positive sample sizes dropped before aggregation
Aggregation numerically correct for a single surviving row
Edge case: nothing survives filtering → zero-row summary, not an error
Missing required columns raise a clear error, not a confusing failure deep inside dplyr/pandas


Case 5 is the one agents most often get wrong on a first draft: ask an agent to write pollster_summary() cold, and there’s a good chance it doesn’t handle the all-filtered-out case at all, or handles it inconsistently (an empty data frame with the wrong columns, or a KeyError/NULL crash). Writing that test before trusting the function is the whole point of this session.
Run them yourself:
Rscript -e ‘testthat::test_file(“scripts/s7/test-pipeline.R”)’
pytest scripts/s7/test_pipeline.py -v

Before running: does each expected value come from your own reasoning, or did the agent just paste back the code’s output? The latter is not a test — it always passes, even after a bug

S8 goes beyond “does this input give this output” into:

Invariants that must hold for any input (property-based testing)
Golden-output comparisons for outputs too complex to hand-compute
Assertions embedded directly in agent-facing scripts

Today’s unit tests are the floor, not the ceiling.

section: Why hardcoded paths break agent workflows
text:
Why hardcoded paths break agent workflows
# R
df <- read.csv("/Users/yourname/Desktop/econ-course/data/houses.csv")
# Python
df = pd.read_csv("/home/yourname/Desktop/econ-course/data/houses.csv")
This works exactly once: on your machine, in that exact location. It breaks the moment:

you move the folder
a classmate clones your repo
an agent is asked to “run this project” from a fresh checkout
you run it from a server that has never seen your filesystem

title: Git + Project Config
text:
The agent angle specifically






Why this matters more with agents


When you hand a repo to an agent and say “run the pipeline,” it infers structure from what it can see: file names, relative paths, a README. A hardcoded absolute path isn’t just non-portable — it’s context the agent cannot reconstruct from the repo alone. It has to fail, notice the failure, and ask where the data really is. That’s a wasted round trip you can eliminate for free.

title: Git + Project Config
section: The fix: resolve paths relative to project root
text:
The fix: resolve paths relative to project root
# R: `here::here()` finds project root via .Rproj / .git,
# regardless of your working directory
library(here)
df <- read.csv(here("data", "houses.csv"))
# Python: build paths relative to the file's own location
from pathlib import Path
DATA_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
df = pd.read_csv(DATA_DIR / "houses.csv")






Exercise 1


Ask your agent to grep your repo for absolute paths (/Users, /home, C:\) and fix every hit using one of the patterns above. Verify by running the scripts from a different working directory than usual.

title: Git + Project Config
text:
Standard project layout
your-project/
├── README.md          # what this is, how to run it, what to expect
├── AGENTS.md           # rules file for coding agents
├── .gitignore
├── data/               # raw + intermediate data
├── R/  or  src/         # source code — functions, not just scripts
├── scripts/            # top-level "run this" entry points
├── tests/              # your S2 tests live here now
├── output/             # figures, tables — generated, not hand-edited
└── prompts/            # archived prompts/sessions
An agent that sees a tests/ folder looks there first, and is more likely to run the existing suite before declaring success. An agent that sees everything dumped flat in the repo root has no such signal — and will guess.






Exercise 2 — restructure your S2 repo


Move your S2 scripts and tests into this layout. Ask your agent to propose the move, then check its work: do scripts still run? Do tests still pass? Did any path silently break?

title: Git + Project Config
text:
README discipline
A README is the first (and sometimes only) context an agent — or a stranger, or you in eight months — gets before touching your code. A good README for this course answers, in order:

What is this? One or two sentences.
How do I run it? The literal commands, in order, from a clean checkout.
What should I see? Expected output — so a wrong result is recognizable as wrong.
What are the parts? A one-line map of the folders, if not obvious.
What does this depend on? R/Python version, packages, any external data.

What a README is not: a changelog, a diary of what you tried, or a copy of your code comments. Keep it short enough that an agent’s context window doesn’t have to spend most of its budget reading prose to find the one command it needs.

title: Git + Project Config
section: Test your README like an agent would
text:
Test your README like an agent would






Try it


Ask your agent — in a fresh session, with no prior context of this project — to read only your README and try to run your pipeline.



If it gets stuck, your README has a gap, not the agent. This is the only reliable way to check “could a stranger pick this up cold” — you already know how your own project works, so you can’t self-assess this one.

title: Git + Project Config
text:
.gitignore discipline
Not everything belongs in version control. Three categories that must never be committed:

Secrets — your S0 LLM API key, any credential. Committing it once means it’s in history forever, even after you delete it.
Large/regenerable data — raw downloads, caches — bloat the repo and aren’t the point of tracking.
Machine-local junk — .DS_Store, .Rproj.user, __pycache__/.

# secrets
.env
*.key

# data (if large / regenerable — document how to get it in README instead)
data/raw/

# machine/tooling junk
.DS_Store
.Rproj.user/
__pycache__/
*.pyc






Check now


Run git log --all --full-history -- "*.env" (or search for any key-shaped string) on your S2 repo. If anything comes back, treat that key as compromised — rotate it.

Project-level agent config: the rules file
OpenCode (and most harnesses) read a project-level instructions file at the repo root — conventionally AGENTS.md. Standing instructions go here instead of being re-typed into every prompt.

## Stack
- R (>= 4.3) and Python (>= 3.11), see README for exact deps.

## Conventions
- No hardcoded absolute paths. Use `here::here()` in R,
  `Path(__file__)`-relative paths in Python.
- Every function in `R/` or `src/` should have a corresponding
  test in `tests/`.

## Before declaring a task done
- Run the test suite (`Rscript tests/run_all.R` or `pytest`) and
  confirm it passes. Do not just say tests would pass.

## Do not touch
- `data/raw/` is read-only — never overwrite raw source data.






Exercise 3 — write your AGENTS.md


Write one for your S2 repo. Keep it short. Then start a fresh agent session and ask for a trivial change. Check whether it actually followed a rule you set (e.g. did it run the tests before saying it was done?).

title: Git + Project Config
text:
Model pinning
“It worked when I tried it” is not reproducible if you don’t know which model you tried it with. Models get updated, deprecated, or silently change behavior server-side.

Record which model + provider you used to build/validate the pipeline (e.g. openrouter/deepseek-v3.2:free, checked 2026-09-20) in your README or AGENTS.md.
If your harness supports pinning a specific model version, do that for anything you intend to reproduce later.
This matters most for S9 (cost) and S11 (reproducibility) — you’re planting the flag now that lets you later answer “did the pipeline change, or did the model change?”

title: Git + Project Config
text:
Prompt archiving
git log records what your code looked like at each commit. It does not record what you asked the agent to get there.
prompts/
├── 2026-09-20-restructure-layout.md
└── 2026-09-20-add-agents-md.md
Each file: the prompt you gave, plus optionally a one-line note on what you had to correct afterward — material you’ll reuse for your S11 checklist.






Why bother


git log answers “what changed.” A prompt archive answers “why” — in an agent-assisted world, “why” often means “what did I ask for.”

title: Git + Project Config
section: Package structure as a reproducibility unit
text:
Package structure as a reproducibility unit
(absorbs old Building R packages — not “how to publish to CRAN,” but “structure is what makes a project reproducible”)
A package (R) or installable module (Python) is the strict, tooling-enforced version of everything above: declared dependencies, fixed internal layout, a built-in place for tests.
R — minimal skeleton:
library(devtools)
create_package("~/myproject")
use_git()
use_r("clean_data")       # creates R/clean_data.R
use_testthat()
use_test("clean_data")    # creates tests/testthat/test-clean_data.R
document()
check()

title: Git + Project Config
text:
Package structure — Python side
myproject/
├── pyproject.toml     # declares deps + build system
├── src/myproject/
│   ├── __init__.py
│   └── clean_data.py
└── tests/
    └── test_clean_data.py
pip install -e .     # editable install
pytest
Common thread: dependencies are declared, not just “whatever happened to be installed,” and tests live where a human and an agent will look for them by convention.






Exercise 4 (optional)


Turn one small function from your S2 scripts into a minimal package/module using the skeleton above, with one test. Full package-publishing depth (vignettes, pkgdown, GitHub Actions CI) is in the r-pkgs book if you want to go further.

title: Git + Project Config
text:
Deliverable
By the end of this session your S2 repo should have:

no hardcoded absolute paths (verify by running from a different working directory)
the standard layout (README.md, AGENTS.md, data/, source folder, tests/)
a .gitignore that keeps secrets and junk out of history
a README a stranger — or a fresh agent session — could follow cold
an AGENTS.md with the conventions you actually want enforced
a note of which model you used to build/validate it
a prompts/ folder with at least one archived prompt from this session

title: Git + Project Config
text:
Key points






Key points



Version control only delivers on reproducibility if the project, not just the code, is portable — no hardcoded paths, declared dependencies, discoverable structure.
.gitignore discipline keeps secrets and junk out of a history you can’t rewrite.
A rules file (AGENTS.md) is durable context: write conventions once, have every agent session read them automatically.
Model identity and prompts are part of your provenance record — you’ll need them in S9 and S11.
Package structure is the strict version of “clean project layout,” useful even if you never publish anything.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Intro






Questions



How can I move around on my computer?
How can I see what files and directories I have?
How can I specify the location of a file or directory on my computer?










Objectives



Explain the similarities and differences between a file and a directory.
Translate an absolute path into a relative path and vice versa.
Construct absolute and relative paths that identify specific files and directories.
Use options and arguments to change the behaviour of a shell command.
Demonstrate the use of tab completion and explain its advantages.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
The File System

The file system organizes data into files and directories on your computer.
let’s start finding out where we are by running the pwd command - present working directory.

$ pwd
with output:
/Users/nelle






Home Directory Variations



Linux: /home/nelle
Windows: C:\Documents and Settings\nelle

if pwd does not return your home directory, may need to navigate there first with cd.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Nelle’s Home Directory
Nelle’s file system looks like this:

The file system is made up of a root directory that contains sub-directories titled bin, data, users, and tmp
/ is the root of the system
all other locations can be reached from there via a path
path to homedir is from / to directory Users, which contains folder Nelle
We know exactly where the home is stored by looking at this path.
Notice that inside a path, / is a separator. (It’s \ on Windows!)

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Working with ls

type ls -F. This adds option F (for full) to the command.
now you get also
a trailing / indicates that this is a directory
@ indicates a link
* indicates an executable

$ ls -F
Applications/ Documents/    Library/      Music/        Public/
Desktop/      Downloads/    Movies/       Pictures/






question


What kind of objects does Nelle’s home directory contain?

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Help






Clear Terminal



Use the clear command to clear terminal.
you can use your ↑ and ↓ keys to see previous commands, or just scroll up.










Getting Help



pass the --help option to a command:

$ ls --Help

Read the manual entry with man (MacOS and Linux only)

man ls 

Search internet for unix man ls

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
More ls Flags






Challenge


You can also use two options at the same time. What does the command ls do when used with the -l option? What about if you use both the -l and the -h option?





Show Solution







Solution


The -l option makes ls use a long listing format, showing not only the file/directory names but also additional information, such as the file size and the time of its last modification. If you use both the -h option and the -l option, this makes the file size ‘human readable’, i.e. displaying something like 5.3K instead of 5369.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
More ls Challenges






Listing in Reverse Chronological Order


By default, ls lists the contents of a directory in alphabetical order by name. The command ls -t lists items by time of last change instead of alphabetically. The command ls -r lists the contents of a directory in reverse order. Which file is displayed last when you combine the -t and -r options? Hint: You may need to use the -l option to see the last changed dates.





Show Solution







Solution


The most recently changed file is listed last when using -rt. This can be very useful for finding your most recent edits or checking to see if a new output file was written.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Getting Data

Let’s download some data
unzip it and and move it to your home directory. (~, not Desktop!)

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Exploring More Directories

ls can search other than only the current directories.
Let’s see what is on our home:

$ cd    # goes HOME
$ ls -F .
shows for Nelle only the data we just downloaded:
shell-lesson-data/

We can also look inside that data from where we are:

$ ls -F shell-less-data
exercise-data/  north-pacific-gyre/

looks intriguing 🧐. Let’s try and go there!

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Going into Subdirectories

cd is for change directory. Moves the shell to a different location in the file system.
Let’s go to our data folder:

$ cd shell-lesson-data 
$ cd exercise-data

Notice that the cd command does not print any output by default.
Run ls -F again to see what’s in this directory!
Run pwd to see where we are!

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Coming Back from Subdirectories

Now we want to go back up one level.
It’s tempting to say cd shell-lesson-data
But cd can only go into its own subdirectories.
It has a special one: .. is its parent directory, so goes one up.

$ cd ..
$ pwd
puts Nelle back into
/Users/nelle/shell-lesson-data

Notice how .. is listed if you flag -a on the ls command.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Hidden Files






Hidden Files



Typing cd without any arguments puts you back into your Home directory. Do it.
Let’s use ls -F -a or ls -Fa to list all files. Also hidden ones!










Relative and Absolute Paths



Up until now, we used relative paths. cd and ls operated from our current position in the file sytem.
We can also specify the absolute path, i.e. starting at the root /. This allows to go anywhere from anywhere.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
More Shortcuts






Tilde (~) and dash (-)



The tilde ~ in first position means current user’s home
The dash in cd - means go into the directory I was previously in.
So:


cd .. brings you up one level
cd - takes you back to wherever you’ve come from.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Challenges






Challenge


Starting from /Users/amanda/data, which of the following commands could Amanda use to navigate to her home directory, which is /Users/amanda?

cd .
cd /
cd /home/amanda
cd ../..
cd ~
cd home
cd ~/data/..
cd
cd ..

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Solution


Show Solution







Solution



No: . stands for the current directory.
No: / stands for the root directory.
No: Amanda’s home directory is /Users/amanda.
No: this command goes up two levels, i.e. ends in /Users.
Yes: ~ stands for the user’s home directory, in this case /Users/amanda.
No: this command would navigate into a directory home in the current directory if it exists.
Yes: unnecessarily complicated, but correct.
Yes: shortcut to go back to the user’s home directory.
Yes: goes up one level.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Solution


Show Solution







Solution



No: there is a directory backup in /Users.
No: this is the content of Users/thing/backup, but with .., we asked for one level further up.
No: see previous explanation.
Yes: ../backup/ refers to /Users/backup/.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Solution


Show Solution







Solution



No: pwd is not the name of a directory.
Yes: ls without directory argument lists files and directories in the current directory.
Yes: uses the absolute path explicitly.

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
General Syntax of Shell Commands
Let’s take as example this command:
$ ls -F /

General syntax of a shell command
The space between ls and whatever options you put is important.
Capitalization is important. ls -s is not the same as ls -S:

$ cd ~/shell-lesson-data
$ ls -s exercise-data  # size
$ ls -S exercise-data  # sort by size

title: Navigating Files and Directories
text:
Nelle’s Pipeline and Tab Completion

Nelle organized the output of the assay machine into north-pacific-gyre/. let’s go there.

$ cd ~/shell-lesson-data/
$ cd north-pacific-gyre

Now north-pacific-gyre is a mouthful to write. try instead to type cd n and hit the TAB key.
hitting TAB twice without any leading character, gives you a list of files in pwd.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Before we start






Assumption


You’ve done 00-prework.qmd: terminal works, git installed, an API key for a free-tier LLM provider, opencode installed and talking to that provider.



If any of that is broken, say so now — we fix it in the first five minutes, not during the lab.






Today’s objectives



Understand four words that get used loosely: model, harness, tool, skill — and why “programming” increasingly means supervising one of these systems rather than typing every line by hand.
Get comfortable enough in a shell to move around, make/edit/delete files, and chain commands.
Initialize a git repo, commit a trivial script, and run one full OpenCode session end to end — reviewing what it did before accepting it.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Why bother with definitions

“AI” and “the model” and “ChatGPT” and “Copilot” get used interchangeably in casual conversation.
That’s fine at a dinner party. It is not fine when you’re debugging why an agent did something weird, or deciding what to pay for.
Four layers, each doing a different job:







The stack


model → harness → tool → skill



We’ll meet each one today at a “what is it” level. How each one works internally is later sessions (S4: models, S5: harnesses/tools).

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
1. The model

A large language model: weights trained to predict the next token, given everything before it.
That’s it — a model, on its own, is a function: text in, text out. It has no memory between calls, can’t read your disk, can’t run anything.
Examples you’re using right now: Gemini, GLM, Qwen, DeepSeek (whichever free-tier one you picked in S0).
Different models = different quality/speed/cost tradeoffs, same basic job.








Not yet


Why next-token prediction produces coherent answers — and why it sometimes confidently produces wrong ones — is S4.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
2. The harness

A model alone can’t do anything to your computer. Something has to:

collect context (your prompt, files, previous turns) and send it to the model,
parse the model’s reply,
actually execute what the model asked for (read a file, run a command, edit code),
show you the result, ask permission where configured to.

That “something” is the harness. In this course: OpenCode.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
2. The harness

Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot Chat, Cline — all harnesses, wrapping different (or the same) models.







Rule of thumb


Same model, different harness → different experience, different capability, sometimes different price.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
3. The tool

A tool is a specific action the harness lets the model invoke: “read this file,” “write this file,” “run this shell command,” “search the web.”
The model doesn’t do these things itself — it emits a structured request (“call read_file with path X”), and the harness executes it and returns the result.
This is why an agent can “see” your repo and “run” your tests: not magic, just tool calls the harness carries out on request.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
4. The skill

A skill is a packaged, reusable set of instructions you (or someone else) hand to the agent so it doesn’t have to reinvent a procedure every time — e.g. “here’s how our team writes commit messages,” “here’s how to structure a test file in this repo.”
Concretely, in OpenCode/Claude-Code-style harnesses: a rules/instructions file the harness reads automatically (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md), or a short standalone procedure you point the agent at.
We’ll write one of these for real in S3 (project config). Today, just recognize the concept: skills are how you encode your own judgment so the agent doesn’t have to guess it fresh each time.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Putting it together






One sentence


You type a prompt → the harness builds context and sends it to the model → the model replies, possibly asking to invoke a tool → the harness runs the tool and loops back → optionally, a skill shaped how the model approached the whole thing.




“Programming with AI” in 2026 mostly means: you supervise this loop. You still need judgment about what’s correct — you just spend less time typing syntax and more time reviewing diffs.
That’s the whole course, really: build the habit of checking what the agent did before you trust it.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Why a shell at all

Agents run in a terminal. If you can’t navigate a filesystem or read a command’s output yourself, you can’t tell whether the agent did the right thing.
We’re not doing a full Software Carpentry pass today — a condensed version. Full reference material (if you want more drills) is linked at the end.
Remember the tradeoff between a GUI and a CLI.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
The filesystem: root, folders, paths

Everything on your machine lives in one tree, starting at the root: / on Mac/Linux, C:\ on Windows.
A folder (= directory) is a node in that tree — it holds files and/or other folders.
Your home folder (~) is where your own stuff lives: /Users/you (Mac), /home/you (Linux).
A path is the address of a file/folder in that tree: list of folders from some starting point, separated by /.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
My filesystem
> tree -L 1 /
/
├── Applications
├── bin
├── cores
├── dev
├── etc -> private/etc
├── home -> /System/Volumes/Data/home
├── Library
├── Network -> /System/Volumes/Data/Network
├── opt
├── private
├── sbin
├── System
├── tmp -> private/tmp
├── Users
├── usr
├── var -> private/var
└── Volumes

Mac: brew install tree
WSL2/Linux: sudo apt install tree

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Where am I, what’s here
$ pwd          # print working directory — where am I?
$ ls           # list what's in the current directory
$ ls -l        # long form: sizes, dates
$ ls -a        # show hidden files too (dotfiles)

pwd and ls are your two most-used commands. Use them constantly, especially right before you let an agent touch anything.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Moving around
$ cd some-directory     # go into a subdirectory
$ cd ..                 # go up one level
$ cd ~                  # go home
$ cd -                  # go back to wherever you just were






Absolute vs relative paths


data/raw.csv is relative to where you are. /Users/you/project/data/raw.csv is absolute — works from anywhere. Agents often produce absolute paths; know the difference so a “file not found” makes sense.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Making and removing things
$ mkdir my-project          # make a directory
$ mkdir -p a/b/c             # make nested directories at once
$ touch script.py            # create an empty file
$ mv old-name.py new-name.py # rename (or move) a file
$ cp script.py backup.py     # copy a file
$ rm backup.py               # delete — no trash bin, this is permanent
$ nano script.py             # edit the file's contents (Ctrl+X to exit, saving)






Editing files


touch creates an empty file; it does not let you type into it. nano is a simple terminal text editor — good enough for today. You’ll likely move to a fuller editor (e.g. VS Code) later, but the shell/agent workflow doesn’t require one.









rm has no undo


There is no recycle bin in the shell. Double-check the path before you hit enter — and definitely before you let an agent run rm on your behalf.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Looking inside files
$ cat script.py       # print the whole file to screen
$ head -n 5 file.csv  # first 5 lines
$ tail -n 5 file.csv  # last 5 lines
$ less file.csv       # scroll interactively (q to quit)

title: S1 — Kickoff
section: How does an agent “search” your code?
text:
How does an agent “search” your code?

When you ask an agent “where is greet defined?” or “find all TODOs,” it doesn’t magically know. It calls a tool (remember Part 1) that searches text.
Under the hood, that tool is almost always some flavor of grep — “global regular expression print.” Harnesses wrap it, but the primitive is this.
So: knowing grep yourself means you can (a) do the same search faster by hand, and (b) tell whether the agent’s “I searched and found nothing” claim is even plausible.

title: S1 — Kickoff
section: Try it: make a file, then search it
text:
Try it: make a file, then search it
$ cat > notes.txt << 'EOF'
TODO: write greet() in hello.py
TODO: add a test for greet()
done: initial commit
GREETING logic lives in hello.py
EOF
Now, before looking ahead — guess what each of these prints, then run it:
$ grep "TODO" notes.txt
$ grep -i "greeting" notes.txt
$ grep -n "done" notes.txt

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
grep: searching inside files
$ grep "greet" hello.py            # lines in hello.py containing "greet"
$ grep -i "greet" hello.py         # case-insensitive
$ grep -n "greet" hello.py         # show line numbers
$ grep -r "TODO" .                 # recursive: search every file under .
$ grep -rl "TODO" .                # recursive, just filenames (not lines)






Why this matters for agents


“Find every place this function is called” is a grep -rn under the hood. If an agent tells you it checked the whole repo, you can run the same grep yourself in two seconds and confirm it isn’t lying or missing a file.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Combining commands: redirection and pipes
$ ls > filelist.txt      # redirect output into a file (overwrite)
$ ls >> filelist.txt     # append instead of overwrite
$ ls -l | head -n 3      # pipe: feed one command's output into the next






Why this matters for agents


Agents live and die by chaining exactly these primitives — reading a file, filtering it, writing a result. If a diff an agent proposes runs a pipeline that looks like line noise, you should now be able to read it left to right.









Want more?


The old, longer walk-throughs — Shell Intro, Files and Directories, Working with Files and Directories, Pipes and Filters — are still in the repo as optional reference material with more worked examples and challenges.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
The goal
By the end of this lab you will have:

A git repository on your machine.
A trivial script inside it, committed.
One complete OpenCode session where you asked the agent to do something, reviewed what it changed, and then committed that too.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Step 1 — make a repo
$ mkdir s1-kickoff && cd s1-kickoff
$ git init

git init turns the current folder into a git repository — a .git/ folder now tracks history here.
We are not doing a git deep-dive today (that’s S3) — just enough to commit something.







First time using git on this machine?


Git refuses to commit until it knows who you are. If git commit later complains “Please tell me who you are,” run this once (only needed the first time ever):
$ git config --global user.name "Your Name"
$ git config --global user.email "you@example.com"

title: S1 — Kickoff
section: Step 2 — write a trivial script, commit it
text:
Step 2 — write a trivial script, commit it
Pick one language — today, use whichever you’re most comfortable reading, Python is a reasonable default.
$ cat > hello.py << 'EOF'
print("hello from s1-kickoff")
EOF
$ python3 hello.py
Then commit it:
$ git add hello.py
$ git commit -m "initial commit: trivial hello script"

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Step 3 — one full OpenCode session
$ opencode
Give it a small, checkable task, for example:
add a function `greet(name)` to hello.py that prints
"hello, <name>, from s1-kickoff" and call it once with your own name
Let it work. Do not accept blindly.

title: S1 — Kickoff
section: Step 4 — review before you trust it
text:
Step 4 — review before you trust it
Before committing what the agent produced:
$ git diff






Ask yourself



Does the diff do only what I asked, nothing more?
Would this code actually run? (run it: python3 hello.py)
Is there anything here I don’t understand? If so, ask the agent to explain the specific line — don’t just accept it.




If it looks right:
$ git add hello.py
$ git commit -m "agent: add greet() via opencode, reviewed"
If it doesn’t look right, tell the agent what’s wrong and iterate — that back-and-forth is the skill this course is teaching.

title: S1 — Kickoff
text:
Checklist — you’re done when

git init repo exists locally, git log shows at least two commits.
hello.py (or equivalent) runs without error.
You ran one OpenCode session that changed a file, and you can point to the exact diff line you checked before accepting it.
You can say, in your own words, what a model, a harness, a tool, and a skill each are — and give one concrete example of each from today.







Next


S2: the same “agent drafts, student verifies” habit, applied to loops/conditionals/functions in both R and Python.
