title: S0 — Before Session 1: Accounts & Install
text:
1. Get a terminal

macOS: open the built-in Terminal app (Spotlight → “Terminal”).
Windows: install WSL2 (Windows Subsystem for Linux) — this gives you a real Linux shell, which is what everything else in this course assumes. Follow: Microsoft’s WSL install guide. One command in PowerShell (as administrator) usually does it:

wsl --install
Restart when prompted, then open the “Ubuntu” app that got installed — that’s your terminal from now on.

Linux: you already have one.

Check it works:
echo "hello from my shell"

title: S0 — Before Session 1: Accounts & Install
text:
2. Install git

macOS: git usually comes with Xcode Command Line Tools. Run git --version; if missing, it will prompt you to install.
WSL2 / Linux: sudo apt update && sudo apt install git -y

Check:
git --version

title: S0 — Before Session 1: Accounts & Install
section: 3. Get a free LLM API key
text:
3. Get a free LLM API key
You do not need a paid subscription for this course. Pick one of these:

OpenRouter (recommended)Google Gemini



Go to openrouter.ai and sign up.
Go to Keys → Create Key. Copy it somewhere safe (you won’t see it again).
OpenRouter gives access to several free-tier models (look for :free suffixed models, e.g. some Gemini, GLM, Qwen, DeepSeek variants). Availability changes — check openrouter.ai/models and filter by price = free.




Go to aistudio.google.com and sign in with a Google account.
Get API key → create a new key. Copy it.
Gemini has a genuinely free tier (rate-limited), no card required.




Either way, do not commit this key to git or paste it in a public chat. Treat it like a password.

title: S0 — Before Session 1: Accounts & Install
text:
4. Install OpenCode
OpenCode is the agent harness we’ll use in class — it’s free and open source, and works with whichever provider/key you picked above (unlike Claude Code, which is tied to Anthropic billing).
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
(macOS with Homebrew also works: brew install sst/tap/opencode)

Nelle Nemo is a marine biologist. 🌊 🐡

Battle Plan

Using a GUI to run goostats.sh, Nelle will have to use her mouse to select and open a file 1520 times.
If goostats.sh takes 30 secs to run, this will take more than 12 hours of Nelle’s active time.
With the help of the shell, Nelle could make her computer go through that list of files instead.

title: The Unix Shell
text:
Key Points



A shell is a program whose primary purpose is to read commands and run other programs.
This lesson uses Bash, the default shell in many implementations of Unix.
Programs can be run in Bash by entering commands at the command-line prompt.
The shell’s main advantages are its high action-to-keystroke ratio, its support for automating repetitive tasks, and its capacity to access networked machines.
The shell’s main disadvantages are its primarily textual nature and how cryptic its commands and operation can be.
ChatGPT can help you write Bash scripts, still it is fundamental to know the basics.

title: Intro to Generic Programming
text:
Variables
Variables are labels for objects. This can be simple numbers, or strings, but often also any other sort of object you could think of: a plot, a table, a matrix, a vector, a list, …
What is curious to know about variables is their scoping behaviour: where in our programs we can we see which variable? This differs quite importantly across languages and is something that requires some thought.
First, let’s create a variable x which holds the value 12.3:

PythonR



x = 12.3
x + 5

17.3





x <- 12.3  # = works also
x + 5

[1] 17.3





Next, a function which will use the variables - here we do not provide x as an argument to the function, so which value will it use in each case?

PythonR



def myfun(y):  
    return x + y  # must use `return`
# note the indentation!
# function definition finishes after last line of indented block.

myfun(8)

20.3





myfun <- function(y){
    x + y  # can use `return()`
}
myfun(8)

[1] 20.3





we see that in both cases, the function looked for the variable x in it’s calling scope, i.e. the environment where it was called from. This only worked because we had defined x before. This may or may not work in other languages. In general this is called lexical scoping.

title: Intro to Generic Programming
text:
Loops
If we have a repetitive task, it’s useful to be able to iterate, i.e. do the same thing to a potentially changing input. Consider that we had 4 numbers 2,3,4,5 and we wanted to print them to screen. We could do of course write 4 identical print statements, each with a different input:

print("this is number",4)
print("this is number",5)

print(paste("this is number",4))
print(paste("this is number",5))

for i in range(2,5) :
    print(f"this is number",i) # note the indentation!

this is number 2
this is number 3
this is number 4





for (i in 2:4){
    print(paste("this is number",i))

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
text:
Where we left off (S7)

S7 gave you unit tests: arrange-act-assert, testthat / pytest, fixtures.
Unit tests answer: “does this one function, called with these inputs, return the value I expect?”
That’s necessary but not sufficient for agent-assisted work, because:

The agent can write a function and a unit test that both agree with each other — and both be wrong.
Some bugs don’t crash and don’t fail an obvious spot-check. They just quietly return a plausible number.

Today: a toolkit for the harder question — “where is this wrong, and how would I even know?”

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
text:
The core problem: plausible-but-wrong
A script that throws an error is not dangerous. You see the error.
A script that runs cleanly and prints 0.42 is dangerous if the correct answer was 0.43 — or worse, 0.30.
Agents are very good at producing code that runs. Running is not the same as correct. Four patterns today, each catching a different flavor of “runs, but wrong”:

Property-based / invariant checks — relationships that must always hold.
Golden-output comparisons — known-correct answers you computed independently.
Embedded assertions — checks living inside the pipeline itself, not just outside it in a test file.
Systematic checks for silent data decisions & hallucinated numbers.

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
text:
Today’s running example
We’ll use a small pipeline over UK Brexit-referendum poll data (data/brexit.csv, 127 polls: remain, leave, undecided shares, samplesize, poll_type).
The pipeline (scripts/s8-pipeline.py / .R) claims to compute the sample-size-weighted average remain share, by poll type.
It contains one seeded bug. You are not told where.






Exercise, running throughout this session


By the end, write a test suite — using today’s four patterns — that catches the bug without being told where it is. Then, only then, look at the pipeline source and see what you found.

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
text:
Pattern 1 — Property-based / invariant checks
Instead of asserting one fixed output, assert a relationship that must hold for any valid input.

“For every poll, remain + leave + undecided is approximately 1.”
“For every poll, the poll’s end date is not after the referendum date.”
“spread equals remain - leave.”

These don’t require knowing the “right” numeric answer. They catch corruption, silent unit errors, and broken joins — the kind of bug that’s invisible until you ask “does this even make sense?”

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
section: Property-based testing with Hypothesis / generated data
text:
Property-based testing with Hypothesis / generated data
Manual invariant checks test the data you happen to have. Property-based testing (Python: hypothesis; R: manual generation is more common, but the idea transfers) generates many random inputs and checks the property holds for all of them — including edge cases you didn’t think to write by hand.
from hypothesis import given, strategies as st

@given(remain=st.floats(min_value=0, max_value=1), n=st.integers(min_value=1, max_value=20))
def test_group_of_identical_polls_averages_to_that_value(remain, n):
    df = make_group(remain=remain, n=n)
    result = weighted_remain_share_by_poll_type(df)
    assert math.isclose(result, remain, abs_tol=1e-9)
If every poll in a group reports the same share, any correctly-weighted average of that group must equal that share exactly. This property holds regardless of weighting — so on its own it won’t catch a bug that only shows up when values differ. That’s a real limitation worth naming: one property test rarely proves correctness, it proves the absence of one class of error.

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
text:
Pattern 2 — Golden-output comparisons
Compute the expected answer independently of the code you’re testing — by hand, in a spreadsheet, from a different tool, or from a trusted prior run — and compare.
GOLDEN_WEIGHTED_REMAIN = {
    "Online": 0.42797727636421834,
    "Telephone": 0.48178425815433584,
}

def test_golden_weighted_remain_share(poll_type, expected):
    got = weighted_remain_share_by_poll_type(polls)[poll_type]
    assert math.isclose(got, expected, abs_tol=1e-4)

Strength: catches any deviation from a known-correct answer, however it happened.
Weakness: you have to trust the golden value. If you compute it with the same bug the pipeline has, the test is worthless. Compute golden values a genuinely different way — different tool, different person, or careful hand arithmetic on a tiny subset.

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
text:
Pattern 3 — Embedded assertions
Not every check belongs in a separate test file. Some belong inside the pipeline, running every time it’s used — including in production, including when an agent runs it unattended.
def weighted_remain_share_by_poll_type(df):
    assert (df["samplesize"] > 0).all(), "zero or negative sample size found"
    assert df["poll_type"].notna().all(), "missing poll_type"
    ...
    result = ...
    assert result.between(0, 1).all(), "share outside [0,1] -- check weighting logic"
    return result

Test files check the code once, when you remember to run them.
Embedded assertions check the data, every single run — which matters most when an agent is calling your pipeline on data you haven’t looked at.
Trade-off: assertions add runtime cost and can be too strict (crashing on legitimately unusual data). Reserve them for invariants you are confident must always hold.
Limitation worth naming up front: assertions like these check that inputs and outputs are sane (positive sample sizes, a share between 0 and 1). They do not check that the computation in between did what its name promises — a wrong-but-plausible number can sail straight through them.

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
section: Pattern 4 — Silent data decisions & hallucinated numbers
text:
Pattern 4 — Silent data decisions & hallucinated numbers
Some of the worst agent-introduced bugs are a function that quietly makes a different decision than its name or docstring promises, and still returns a plausible-looking number. Two classic examples:

A merge/join with the wrong key silently drops or duplicates rows — the row count still looks “about right”.
A function named weighted_average(...) that, somewhere in its body, forgets to actually use the weight column — the result is still a valid average, just not the average it claims to be.

The systematic check: recompute the same quantity a genuinely different way, and compare — don’t just check the output is plausible, check how it was derived.
# generic pattern, illustrative -- not today's exact case
result = some_pipeline_function(df)
independent = recompute_the_same_quantity_a_different_way(df)
assert abs(result - independent) < tolerance
This is the pattern that most directly targets hallucinated numbers from an agent: an LLM-written aggregation can be internally consistent and still not compute what its own name says it computes.

title: S8 — Testing & Verification, Part 2: Verification Patterns
text:
Exercise (do this now)

Open scripts/s8-pipeline.py (or .R) — read the function signatures and docstrings, but resist the urge to hand-trace every line yet.
Using the four patterns above, write tests in a new file that you believe would catch a bug in this pipeline, before you’re sure exactly what it is.
Run your tests. Do any fail?
Now read the implementation of weighted_remain_share_by_poll_type line by line. Did your tests target the actual bug? If not, which pattern would have?
Compare with the instructor reference: scripts/test_s8_pipeline.py (Python) / scripts/test-s8-pipeline.R (R). Note which of its tests fail against the buggy pipeline — that’s the toolkit doing its job.

Both numbers are inside [0, 1]. Both look like sane poll averages. Nothing crashes, and the pipeline’s own embedded assertions (share in [0,1], positive sample sizes) stay silent — they check the data is sane, not that the formula is the one advertised. Only a check that knows what the correct computation should have been — golden value or independent recomputation — catches it. title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Intro
In this session we cover geospatial data and how to handle it with R — but the point is not “learn sf syntax by hand.” The point is: spatial bugs are often silent. A map with the wrong projection, a distance computed by hand on raw lon/lat coordinates instead of a projected one — these still look like a map or a plausible number. Nothing crashes. Nothing looks obviously wrong. You have to know what to check — and, just as importantly, which operations already check for you and which don’t.






tl;dr


Yes, R is a fully fledged GIS. No, you don’t need an ArcGIS (or other) license to do real work with spatial data.
Today: you’ll ask your agent (OpenCode) to propose CRS transforms and spatial joins. You verify every one against a plotted map and a known fact (an area, a distance, a row count) — because “it looks like a map” is not verification.




Resources

Geocomputation with R is our main reference.
The sf package vignettes are outstanding.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Why Spatial Bugs Are Different


Most bugs you’ve met so far (S2, S7, S8) announce themselves: wrong number, failed test, crashed script.




Some don’t: hand-computing a distance from raw lon/lat coordinates instead of routing through a projected CRS gives you a plausible-looking number in the wrong units, with no error and no warning.




A projection mistake changes areas and distances by a scale factor, but the map still looks like a recognizable outline of the country.




Others do announce themselves — st_join() on mismatched CRS refuses to run rather than silently mis-joining. Knowing which operations protect you and which don’t is itself part of the skill.









Warning


Rule for today: never accept an agent’s spatial code because “the plot looks right.” Always check it against something you can independently compute or already know (a real distance, a known area, an expected row count).

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Spatial Data Basics

One prime example of spatial data are of course maps, providing an answer to the age-old question where is what.
Fundamentally, spatial data still provide an answer to the same question, it is just that the what part has gotten much richer over the years.
The attribute location may be only one of many other features of information on a certain observation.
Multiple measurements imply that observations can be observed moving in space.
There are two fundamentally different ways in which to consider spatial data:

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Spatial Data Types








1. Vector Data


We represent things with points, lines and polygons. We can scale and stretch and transform those easily with mathematical operations. Can increase precision to arbitrary levels (can always zoom in further).












2. Raster Data


We have fixed-size tiles or cells (like a mosaic, or like pixels), which form a grid. Fixed resolution.







This lecture deals mostly with Vector Data (see the pointers at the end for Raster Data).

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Representation of Vector Data


Basically, we concentrate on a 2-dimensional space, even though three-dimensional spaces can be useful as well (any ideas for examples?)




In other words, we denote a location with a tuple of coordinates \((x,y)\), or \((x,y,z)\) as the case may be, where each coordinate gives the distance from the origin in each direction. For example, we could represent Paris by the tuple c(2.34,48.85)




One key question in the context of spatial data concerning planet earth you should ask is: Where is the Origin?




Another question is, related to the well known fact that the earth is quasi-ellipsoid (i.e. a bit like a squashed football and — just to be sure: not flat), how to represent locations in three dimensions on a 2-dimensional map?

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Coordinate Reference Systems (CRS)


CRSs use longitude and latitude to identify locations.




One widely used CRS is the World Geodetic System 1984, or WGS84 (used on google maps). It measures angular distance in degrees in a geocentric datum (made for the entire planet).




longitude measures East-West distance from the Prime Meridian Plane. (left-to-right distance from a starting point)




latitude measures North-South distance of Equatorial Plane. (up-down distance from a starting point)









Important


This is exactly the kind of thing an agent will get subtly wrong: mixing a geographic CRS (degrees) with a projected CRS (meters) in the same computation. Both “work” — neither errors out — but only one gives you a sensible distance in km.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
One Standard CRS: WGS84





The dashed lines are the WGS84 ellipsoid coordinate frame
The blue circle is the origin at \((0,0)\):

0 degrees longitude (x-direction): Prime Meridian through Greenwich, London.
0 degrees latitude (y-direction): Equator.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Paris in Different CRS





Paris at c(2.34,48.85) in WGS84






Paris at c(600256.4, 127726.4) in NTF Lambert North France



Same city, two totally different-looking numbers. Neither is “wrong” — but you cannot add, subtract, or compute distances across the two without transforming first.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Geocentric vs Local Datum

Figure from Geocomputation with R. Geocentric and local geodetic datums shown on top of a geoid (in false color and the vertical exaggeration by 10,000 scale factor). Image of the geoid is adapted from the work of Ince et al. (2019)

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
The Workflow For Today


You state the task in plain language (e.g. “join the Seine river network to French administrative regions and plot which regions it flows through”).




The agent (OpenCode) proposes R code using sf: reads the data, checks/transforms CRS, does the join, plots it.




You verify — not by eyeballing the plot alone, but by checking: same CRS on both inputs? sensible row count after the join? a known distance/area come out close to the real value?









Warning


If step 3 fails, you go back to the agent with what you found — not “it’s wrong,” but “the join produced 40 rows when there should be at most 12, I bet the CRS didn’t match before the join.”

text:
Working with sf 3: A Choropleth

Works also with ggplot2 — this is our first choropleth, a map shaded by a variable value.


library(ggplot2)
ggplot(nc) + geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA)) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Area")


Verification check: does AREA here have sensible units? North Carolina is roughly 139,000 km². Look at range(nc$AREA) — if the numbers don’t come close to plausible, something about the units or CRS is off before you even get to the transform step.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Prompt Task 1: CRS Transform


Ask your agent:

“Take the nc sf object and reproject it to the Mollweide projection (+proj=moll). Plot both the original and reprojected AREA choropleth side by side.”

Then verify:

Did the agent use st_transform(), not just relabel the CRS with st_set_crs()? (The latter is the classic silent bug — it changes the label, not the coordinates.)
Check st_crs(nc) before and after — did it actually change?
Do the two maps look like genuinely different projections of the same shape (not just a re-scaled or shifted copy)?



library(dplyr)
ggplot(nc) + geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA)) +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Area")







nc |>
    st_transform("+proj=moll") |>
    ggplot() + geom_sf(aes(fill = AREA)) +
        scale_fill_viridis_c(name = "Area") +
        ggtitle("Mollweide Projection")

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Geometric Operations with sf

The simple features standard specifies a series of operations.
The relevant functions start with st_ (for spatio-temporal): st_distance(x,y), st_intersection(x,y), st_area(x), st_union(x), st_buffer(x,dist), st_centroid(x), etc.


st_area(st_union(nc))

127025870730 [m^2]



That number is in m², which is not very readable. Ask the agent to convert to km² — a correct answer uses units::set_units(), not a hand-rolled /1e6 (which breaks silently if the CRS units aren’t meters to start with).


st_area(st_union(nc)) |> units::set_units(km2)

127025.9 [km^2]


Verification check: North Carolina’s land area is about 126,000 km² (roughly 139,000 km² including water). If your agent’s number is off by orders of magnitude, suspect a CRS/units mismatch, not arithmetic.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
section: Mapping the Seine: Setting Up the Join
text:
Mapping the Seine: Setting Up the Join
We now build a real spatial-join example: French administrative regions, joined against the Seine/Marne/Yonne river network.

sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)


This specific polygon data (a maps-package outline) has a ring that the default spherical (s2) geometry engine considers invalid; switching to the older planar GEOS engine tolerates it. This is itself an “ask your agent why” moment — checklist item 5 below.


# install.packages(c("maps","spData"))
france = st_as_sf(maps::map('france', plot = FALSE, fill = TRUE))
data("seine", package = "spData")







Important


This is exactly the moment to prompt-check your agent. Ask it: “before you join france and seine, print st_crs(france) and st_crs(seine) — are they the same?” If the agent skips this and jumps straight to st_join(), push back — that’s the step worth double-checking.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Mapping the Seine: The Fix

## Make sure they have the same projection
seine = st_transform(seine, crs = st_crs(france))

pseine = ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = france, alpha = 0.8, fill = "black", col = "gray50") +
  geom_sf(data = seine, col = "#05E9FF", lwd = 1) +
  labs(title = "Administrative regions of France",
       subtitle = "Also showing the Seine, Marne and Yonne rivers")

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
section: Spatial Join: Which Regions Does the Seine Flow Through?
text:
Spatial Join: Which Regions Does the Seine Flow Through?

pl4 = st_join(france, seine) |>
  ## Get rid of regions with no overlap
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(name)) |>
  ## Some regions are duplicated b/c two
  ## branches of the river network flow through them
  dplyr::distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(alpha = 0.5, fill = "#01731f", col = "#fcb4b3", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_sf(data = seine, col = "#05E9FF", lwd = 1) +
  labs(title = "Intersected regions only") +
  theme_bw()

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
section: The Seeded Bug: Not Every Operation Protects You
text:
The Seeded Bug: Not Every Operation Protects You
Here is a version of this exact join, as an agent might first hand it back to you — with the CRS-fix step dropped:

## Reload a fresh, untransformed copy — this demo shouldn't depend on
## whether you ran the (eval:false) fix chunk above in your own session.
data("seine", package = "spData")

## BUG: no st_transform() before the join — seine is still in its
## original CRS, france is in whatever maps::map() returns.
pl_bug = st_join(france, seine) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(name))

Error in `st_geos_binop()`:
! st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE



Good news, this time: st_join() checks that both inputs share a CRS and refuses to run rather than silently matching on whatever coordinates it has — you get st_crs(x) == st_crs(y) is not TRUE immediately, not a plausible-looking-but-wrong map. That’s sf protecting you. Not every spatial computation is this well-behaved — the next section shows one that isn’t.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
section: A Genuinely Silent Bug: Distance Without Projecting
text:
A Genuinely Silent Bug: Distance Without Projecting

A typical question: what’s the straight-line distance between the centroids of the Seine-Maritime and Nièvre départements?
st_distance() itself is CRS-aware — it does the sensible thing even on unprojected lon/lat input. But nothing stops an agent (or you) from reaching past it: pulling raw coordinates with st_coordinates() and hand-computing a Euclidean distance directly. That version has no error, no warning, and just returns a number — in degrees, silently mistaken for kilometers.


pl = st_join(france, st_transform(seine, crs = st_crs(france))) |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(name)) |>
  dplyr::distinct(ID, .keep_all = TRUE)

subdeps = pl |> dplyr::filter(ID %in% c("Seine-Maritime", "Nievre"))
cents = st_centroid(subdeps)

## BUG: hand-rolled Euclidean distance on raw lon/lat coordinates,
## silently treated as if it were kilometers.
xy = st_coordinates(cents)
naive_dist = sqrt(sum(diff(xy)^2))

## Correct: project to a metric CRS first, then use st_distance().
correct_dist = subdeps |>
  st_transform(2154) |>
  st_centroid() |>
  st_distance() |>
  units::set_units("km")

naive_dist

[1] 3.542147

correct_dist

Units: [km]
         [,1]     [,2]
[1,]   0.0000 336.5977
[2,] 336.5977   0.0000


Verification check: the real straight-line distance between these two départements’ centroids is roughly 335–340 km — two independent routes (a projected planar distance and a great-circle distance on the unprojected coordinates) agree within a couple of km of each other. naive_dist above comes out around 3.5 — two orders of magnitude off, because it’s a difference measured in degrees, not km. Nothing in that computation errors or warns; you only catch it by checking against an outside number.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Task: Catch the Silent One

Ask your agent for the straight-line distance between two départements’ centroids, without mentioning the projection pitfall.
Check whether it routed the computation through a projected CRS and st_distance(), or hand-computed coordinates directly. Either can look like a normal, plausible number — that’s the point of a silent bug.
Verify the result both ways: (a) plot the two centroids and a connecting line — does it look right on the map? — and (b) check the number against an outside source (a map-ruler estimate, a second computation route).
Write down, in your own words: what did the wrong version’s number look like, and what specific check caught it? This is the “one case you had to correct” for this session’s outcome.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Task: Distances, Verified
Modifying the join from before, ask your agent to produce two plots:

One that colors only the two named départements and marks their centroids.
Another with a straight line connecting both centroids, printing the distance in km in the plot title.







Figure 1







Figure 2






Desired outputs



Then verify the printed distance against an independent source (e.g. a quick search for the two départements’ préfectures and a rough map-ruler estimate) before you trust it.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
Choropleth + Join, Put Together
This session’s outcome is a correct choropleth or spatial join you can explain end-to-end, including the one case you had to correct. A minimal checklist to walk through with your own agent-produced map:


CRS check: did you print st_crs() on every input before combining them?




Transform, don’t relabel: st_transform() changes coordinates; st_set_crs() only changes the label. An agent using the latter to “fix” a mismatch is a bug, not a fix.




Row-count sanity: after a join, does the row count match what you’d expect (not exploded by duplicate matches, not collapsed to zero)?




Independent number: does at least one summary statistic (area, distance, count) match something you can verify outside the code — a real-world fact, a back-of-envelope estimate, or a value from a different tool?




Can you explain it? If your agent used a function you don’t recognize (e.g. sf_use_s2()), ask it to explain why it was necessary before moving on.

title: Spatial Data, Agent-Native
text:
What’s Different?

We have a grid (pixels) where each cell contains one single data value — usually our measure of interest.
We can have multiple layers of measurements (e.g. temperature, humidity and elevation for a grid cell).
CRS considerations equally apply — and so does the same discipline: verify before you trust.
Remote Sensing Data (e.g. Satellite images) are often in raster format.

title: S11 — Reproducibility & Failure Modes
text:
Why this session exists

Remote session — no lecture, a debrief, a standard, and a personal document you write and keep
By now (S4–S10) an agent has almost certainly produced something that looked right and wasn’t
That’s not hypothetical — it’s the single most reliable thing about working with LLMs


That is the reason this course spends two full sessions (S7, S8) on testing before circling back to it here. This page connects two things usually taught separately: (1) what a professional reproducibility standard actually demands — the lens I use as Data Editor of the Journal of Political Economy when checking whether an accepted paper’s results can be regenerated from its code and data; (2) what you have personally already seen go wrong in this course, and what caught it.







Objectives



Understand what a journal-grade replication package requires, and why each requirement exists.
Catalogue every case in S4–S10 where an agent produced a plausible-but-wrong result, and identify what caught it.
Write a personal checklist you will actually use the next time an agent writes code for you.

title: S11 — Reproducibility & Failure Modes
text:
Part 1 — The Data Editor’s lens
When a paper is conditionally accepted at a journal like the JPE, authors submit a replication package: code, data, documentation — sufficient for someone uninvolved to regenerate every table and figure.
My job as Data Editor: check whether that’s actually true, not whether the authors say it’s true.

The standard is not exotic. It is a small number of concrete requirements, each of which maps onto a failure mode you have already lived through in this course.

title: S11 — Reproducibility & Failure Modes
section: The standard, mapped to failure modes
text:
The standard, mapped to failure modes








Requirement
What it checks
Failure mode it prevents




One-command run
No private “the trick” knowledge needed
Code that only runs on the author’s machine


Pinned versions
Results don’t silently drift
“Worked yesterday”


No hardcoded paths
Runs on any machine
/Users/you/Desktop/data.csv (S3’s requirement)


Data provenance
Every input traceable
Silent undocumented filtering upstream


README
Stranger finds code → output mapping
Nobody, incl. you in 6 months, can find how it was made


Seeds set
Exactly reproducible stochastics
Results that quietly drift each run


Auditable sample construction
Every row-drop visible & justified
Silent sample-selection changes the answer




Notice what this standard is really about: it does not ask “is the code good style” or “is the paper’s argument correct.” It asks can this specific, exact result be regenerated by someone who is not you, using only what you gave them. That is a narrower and more mechanical question than “is this correct” — and it is exactly the right question to ask about anything an agent wrote, because an agent will happily hand you code that runs, produces a plausible number, and is only correct by accident, once, on your machine, with your data. This is also why S3 made you restructure your repo (paths, README, config) before you had a “publication” to worry about: reproducibility discipline is infrastructure you build in from session one, not a checklist you apply retroactively to a finished project.

title: S11 — Reproducibility & Failure Modes
text:
Part 2 — Debrief: the failure log
Across S4–S10 you used agents for: scripts (S2), a DuckDB pipeline (S6), unit tests (S7), invariant/property checks + seeded-bug hunt (S8), spatial joins/CRS (S10), cost/scale reasoning (S9).
Task: go back through your own work and fill in the table with at least four real entries — not hypothetical.

S4 gave you the underlying reason all of this happens: hallucination is a structural property of how an LLM generates text, not an occasional glitch. If you genuinely cannot find four entries, that is itself informative — it usually means you weren’t checking closely enough, and you should look again, harder, before concluding the agent was flawless four sessions running.

title: S11 — Reproducibility & Failure Modes
text:
The failure log template










Session
What the agent produced
Why plausible
What caught it
Could S7/S8-style test catch it?




e.g. S6
Join silently dropped unmatched rows
Ran without error, row count “looked reasonable”
Manual row-count check before/after join
Yes — row-count invariant

























For each row, be specific about the mechanism: was it a hallucinated number (S4: the model predicted a plausible-sounding token, not a looked-up fact)? A silent unit/CRS mismatch (S10: the map “looked fine” at first glance)? A test that passed but tested the wrong thing (S7/S8: arrange-act-assert on the wrong assertion)? A cost/scale estimate that assumed the wrong pricing tier (S9)? Naming the mechanism is what turns this from a diary into a diagnostic tool — it’s the difference between “the agent was wrong” and “the agent was wrong in this particular, recognizable way.” If you cross-reference against your S7/S8 test suite: does a test already exist that would have caught this case? If not, is it worth adding one? You do not have to add it now, but note whether it’s the kind of thing a test could catch (an invariant, a golden-output comparison, a row-count check) versus the kind of thing that fundamentally requires a human to look at output and judge whether it’s sensible (a spatial join that “looks like a map” but uses the wrong projection — S10’s example of a silent bug that survives casual inspection).

What’s the cheapest check you can run every time, versus the expensive check you’ll only run before something ships (a presentation, a submission, handing code to a collaborator)? title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Where we are

S1–S3: you’ve been using an agent — shell, git, project config.
Before we go deeper into how agents operate (S5: context windows, tool calls, harnesses), we need to understand the thing underneath the agent.
Today: no code. Just enough of the machinery to reason correctly about what an LLM can and cannot do.







Goal for today


By the end, you can explain — at a dinner party, without hand-waving — why an LLM can state a wrong number with total confidence.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
The claim we’re testing

“The model said the paper was published in 2019. It’s actually 2017. Why would it just make that up?”


This is the single most common failure mode you’ll hit using agents in this course.
It is not a bug that a future model version will “fix.”
It is a direct, structural consequence of what these models are and how they’re trained.
Today’s lecture is entirely in service of justifying that last sentence.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Text isn’t the input

You type words. The model never sees words.
Text is first chopped into tokens — sub-word chunks from a fixed vocabulary (tens of thousands of entries), typically learned from a large text corpus so common chunks (like ing, tion, whole common words) each get their own token.
Example, roughly how a tokenizer might split a sentence:

"Unbelievable coincidences happen."
→ ["Un", "believ", "able", " coincid", "ences", " happen", "."]

Rare words get split into several tokens; common words often are one token. Numbers are frequently split in unintuitive ways.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Why this matters already

A model doesn’t “see” the number 47293 as one thing. It might see it as tokens ["472", "93"] or ["47", "293"] depending on the tokenizer.
Arithmetic, character counts (“how many r’s in strawberry?”), and precise quoting are all harder than they look because of tokenization, before we’ve even gotten to prediction or training.
Everything downstream operates on tokens, not characters, not words, not “meaning” in any human sense — yet.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
The one task

An LLM is trained to do exactly one thing: given a sequence of tokens, predict a probability distribution over the next token.

\[
P(\text{next token} \mid \text{all tokens so far})
\]

That’s it. Not “understand,” not “reason,” not “know facts.” Predict what token comes next, given everything that came before.
Generating a whole response is just: predict one token, append it, predict the next one, repeat — over and over, one token at a time.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
From distribution to text

At each step the model outputs a probability over the entire vocabulary — not a single answer.
A sampling strategy picks the actual next token:

Greedy: always pick the single most likely token.
Sampling with temperature: pick randomly, weighted by probability; higher temperature → more randomness/variety, lower → more deterministic and repetitive.

This is why asking the same question twice can give you different (but both fluent) answers — you’re sampling from a distribution, not looking up a stored fact.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
A key consequence, stated plainly

The model is not consulting a database and reporting what it finds.
It is producing the most statistically plausible continuation of the text so far, token by token.
Plausible-sounding and true are correlated (because true things are usually written down more, and in more consistent ways) — but they are not the same property, and nothing in the mechanism guarantees they coincide.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
The problem it solves

To predict the next token well, the model needs to weigh which earlier tokens matter for this particular prediction.
In “The trophy didn’t fit in the suitcase because it was too big” — what does “it” refer to? You need to relate a token to other tokens far away in the sentence, and the relevant one changes depending on context.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Attention, the conceptual version

Every token, at every layer, gets to “look back” at every token that came before it (never ahead — this is a one-directional, left-to-right model) and ask: how relevant are you to me, right now?
That one-directional constraint is exactly why generation happens left-to-right, one token at a time: the model was built and trained to only ever condition on what’s already there.
This produces a weighted blend: each token’s representation gets updated using information pulled from the tokens most relevant to it.
Stack many of these attention layers on top of each other (this is the “transformer” — dozens of layers is typical), each one refining the representation a bit further, mixing local grammar-level patterns in early layers with more abstract, longer-range relationships in later ones.
No memory, no lookup table, no symbolic reasoning module. Just repeated rounds of “which other tokens should influence how I update this one,” turned into more predictive representations for the final next-token-probability step.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
section: Why “conceptual level” is the right level
text:
Why “conceptual level” is the right level

You do not need the matrix algebra to reason correctly about LLM behavior in this course.
You do need to internalize: the model is a very large, learned function that transforms a sequence of tokens into a probability distribution over the next token, by repeatedly mixing information across positions.
There is no separate “fact-checking module,” no “I don’t know this” circuit, no built-in notion of source or citation. Whatever behavior looks like those things is emergent from next-token prediction, not a distinct mechanism bolted on.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Stage 1: pretraining

Train the next-token-prediction task on an enormous corpus of text (a large fraction of the public internet, books, code, etc.).
The model has no notion of “this document is reliable” and “this one is not” — it’s fitting probability to co-occurrence patterns in text, at massive scale.
Result: a model that is very good at producing fluent, plausible continuations of almost any text — but has no built-in preference for “true” over “plausible,” and no mechanism forcing it to say “I don’t know.”

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Stage 2: instruction tuning + RLHF

Raw pretrained models complete text; they don’t naturally “answer a question” or “follow an instruction” the way a chat assistant does.
Instruction tuning: further training on examples of (instruction → good response) pairs, so the model learns the chat assistant behavior pattern.
RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback): humans (or another model trained to imitate human preferences) rank candidate responses; the model is further nudged to produce outputs that raters prefer.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
section: What RLHF optimizes for — and what it doesn’t
text:
What RLHF optimizes for — and what it doesn’t

Raters tend to prefer answers that are confident, complete, well-formatted, and decisive over answers that hedge, refuse, or say “I’m not sure.”
This creates real pressure toward fluent, confident-sounding output, independent of the pressure toward correct output.
Nothing in this pipeline directly optimizes for “calibrated uncertainty” unless it is specifically and carefully trained for — and even then, imperfectly.
Put bluntly: the training process rewards sounding right at least as much as being right.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Live demo — watch it happen






Instructor demo, no student setup needed


Open OpenCode with the free-tier model and ask it a question with a precise, checkable answer in an area we know cold — e.g. “give me the exact page number and DOI for [a specific paper],” or “what was the exact closing value of [some index] on [a specific past date].”




Watch it answer immediately, confidently, and specifically — a real-looking DOI, a real-looking page number.
Then check it. It’s very likely wrong, but phrased exactly like a right answer would be phrased.
Keep this moment in mind — Part 5 is the explanation for what you just watched.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Putting the pieces together

The model’s only job, at the mechanical level, is next-token prediction — a plausibility judgment, not a truth judgment.
It has no lookup table or citation mechanism; “knowledge” is encoded implicitly as statistical patterns compressed across billions of parameters, not stored as retrievable facts with sources attached.
RLHF further rewards confident, fluent, complete-sounding answers.
Sampling introduces genuine randomness into which plausible continuation gets picked.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
The structural conclusion

When the true answer and a plausible-sounding wrong answer are both consistent with the patterns the model has seen, the model has no internal mechanism that reliably tells the difference — because “look up whether this is true” was never the task it was trained on.
A model producing a wrong number with total confidence is not “malfunctioning.” It is doing exactly what it was built and trained to do: emit the most probable-sounding continuation, phrased the way confident answers are usually phrased.
This is why “wait for the next model version to fix hallucination” is the wrong mental model. Bigger and better-trained models hallucinate less often, and about narrower categories of things — but the mechanism guaranteeing it can’t happen doesn’t exist and can’t be patched in without changing what the model fundamentally is.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
What actually reduces hallucination (preview)

These are compensating strategies bolted on around the model, not fixes to the model itself:

Giving the model the actual source in context, so it can “quote” rather than “recall” (retrieval-augmented generation) — this is one reason context windows matter, which we pick up in S5.
Tool use: letting the model call a calculator, a search engine, or code execution instead of predicting the answer token-by-token (also S5).
Verification: the student/researcher checks claims rather than trusting fluency — this is the whole point of S7/S8 in this course.

None of these make the underlying mechanism “know” things. They change what information is available to condition the next-token prediction on, or add an external check the model itself doesn’t have.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Take-home (the dinner-party version)






The one paragraph you should be able to say out loud


An LLM doesn’t look anything up — it predicts, one chunk of text at a time, whatever continuation is statistically most plausible given everything written before it, based on patterns learned from huge amounts of text. Its training additionally rewards sounding confident and complete. So when it doesn’t actually “know” a fact, nothing stops it from generating a wrong one that’s phrased exactly like a right one — because from the model’s point of view, both are just “plausible next tokens.” That’s why you always verify, especially numbers, dates, and citations.

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Your turn






60 seconds, then say it out loud


Turn to your neighbour. Using the demo you just watched, explain in your own words why the model gave a confident, specific, wrong answer. Don’t read the callout above — try it cold.




Two volunteers explain it to the room.
If your explanation mentions “the model looked it up and got it wrong,” that’s the misconception this lecture exists to correct — try again using “predict” instead of “look up.”

title: S4 — How Do LLMs Actually Work?
text:
Where this leads next

S5: given this picture of the model, how does an agent built on top of it work — context windows, tool calling, system prompts?
S7/S8: given that hallucination is structural, how do you build habits and tests that catch it, systematically, rather than by luck?
S11: a running catalogue, across the whole course, of every place this bit you — and what caught it.

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
Where we are

S4: how an LLM actually works (tokens in, tokens out, no ground truth inside).
S5: how an agent wraps that model with tools, context, and a harness.
Today the tool is a database, and the task is data wrangling: getting from raw files to trustworthy numbers.







Today’s habit, again


The agent will happily write a query that runs without error and returns a plausible number. Running without error is not the same as being right.

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
Today’s plan

What DuckDB is, and why it is a good fit for this course.
One dataset, three ways to query it: SQL, dplyr, Ibis.
Let the agent draft a query. Find out it’s wrong. Fix it.
You do the same, on your own query, and write it down.

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
DuckDB in one slide

An in-process analytical (OLAP) SQL database — like SQLite, but built for aggregations over large columnar data instead of many small transactions.
No server to install, no daemon to start: import duckdb (Python), library(duckdb) (R), or the duckdb CLI binary.
Reads CSV / Parquet / JSON directly, without a separate load step:

SELECT * FROM 'data/brexit.csv' LIMIT 5;

Fast, columnar, and free — a real analytical engine on your laptop.

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
Why DuckDB for this course


R and Python both talk SQL fluently through DuckDB — it’s a genuine common ground between the two languages this course uses.




The same question can be asked three ways:

raw SQL — the lingua franca, and what the agent tends to reach for first.
dplyr verbs (R) translated to SQL under the hood.
Ibis expressions (Python) translated to SQL under the hood.





All three compile to the same DuckDB query plan. If they disagree, one of you (or the agent) made a mistake — that disagreement is itself a verification tool.

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
Setup


SQL / CLI
duckdb

R
library(duckdb)
library(dplyr)
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())
polls <- tbl(
  con,
  "read_csv_auto('data/brexit.csv')"
)

Python
import duckdb
import ibis

con = ibis.duckdb.connect()
polls = con.read_csv(
  "data/brexit.csv",
  table_name="polls"
)

All three point at the same file — no import/export, no separate database to keep in sync.

section: Ask the agent: “what does this data predict?”
text:
Ask the agent: “what does this data predict?”
Prompt given to the agent (OpenCode):

“Write a DuckDB SQL query against data/brexit.csv that estimates the referendum outcome — the percentage voting Leave and the percentage voting Remain.”

The agent’s first draft — plausible, runs without error:
SELECT
  round(avg(leave)  * 100, 2) AS leave_pct,
  round(avg(remain) * 100, 2) AS remain_pct
FROM 'data/brexit.csv';

text:
Verify before you trust it
The cheapest check costs one extra line: do the shares add up to 100%?

leave_pct
remain_pct

They do (≈100%, modulo rounding) — but the query silently dropped undecided respondents from the two numbers it reported. leave_pct + remain_pct alone is only 86.5%, not 100%. The agent answered the wrong question: “average raw share” instead of “share of those who expressed a preference.”

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
What actually went wrong


No re-normalization: it reported leave and remain shares out of all respondents (including undecided), not as shares of decided voters — the quantity we actually asked for.




No weighting: AVG() treats a poll of 500 people the same as a poll of 5,000 — every poll gets an equal vote, regardless of samplesize.




No date filtering: it averaged polls from January and June together, as if opinion in January (5+ months before the vote) were as informative as opinion the week before.


None of these threw an error. All three are silent, plausible-looking mistakes — exactly the kind unit tests and invariant checks (S7–S8) are built to catch.

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
Check against the known answer

Fixed query, final week of polling: Leave ≈ 48.6%, Remain ≈ 51.4%.
Actual result: Leave 51.89%, Remain 48.11%.







The query is now correct. The prediction is still wrong.


Fixing the SQL bug (undecided handling, weighting, date window) got us a defensible number — but it’s still on the wrong side of the actual outcome. 2016 UK polls famously under-counted Leave support (non-response bias, “shy” Leave voters, herding among pollsters).



This is the distinction to keep: verification catches query bugs (wrong denominator, wrong weights, wrong date range — things you can check against an invariant). It does not catch measurement error in the data itself — that needs domain knowledge, not a better query. Keep this distinction for S9 (cost/quality tradeoffs) and S11 (cataloguing failure modes).

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
Exercise (20 min)
Working with the same brexit.csv (or a dataset of your choice with a known, checkable answer):

Give your agent a data question and let it draft a first query — SQL, dplyr, or Ibis, your choice.
Run it. Get a number.
Before you believe it, write down at least one check: does it sum to what it should? Does it match a known external fact? Does a second language (SQL vs. dplyr vs. Ibis) give the same answer?
If the first answer fails a check, find out why, fix the query, and re-run.

Ideas to try: split by pollster or poll_type (phone vs. online — did they differ systematically?), compute a rolling weekly average, or compare spread in the data to leave - remain you compute yourself (does the pollster’s number match your recomputation?).

text:
Deliverable: the written note
For the session outcome, write down one concrete case where the agent’s first answer was wrong, in this format:






Template



Prompt you gave the agent.
First query it produced (SQL/dplyr/Ibis).
First output — the specific wrong number(s).
How you caught it — the check that failed (invariant, known answer, cross-language comparison, or something else).
Fixed query and the corrected output.




This is not a hypothetical exercise — use whatever actually happened when you ran your own prompt. If your agent got it right first try, push it further (harder aggregation, trickier date logic, a join) until it doesn’t.

title: Data Wrangling: DuckDB
text:
Wrap-up

DuckDB gives you one query engine reachable from SQL, R (dplyr), and Python (Ibis) — no data export/import between them.
The agent’s first query is a draft, not an answer. It ran without error and still ignored undecided respondents, sample weights, and the relevant date window.
Checking against an invariant (do shares sum to 100%?) or a known external fact (the actual referendum result) is cheap and catches real bugs.
Even a correct query only answers the question you asked — it can’t fix bias in the underlying data.
Next (S7): turning these ad-hoc checks into a proper, repeatable test suite.
